course.title: Analytics Engineering and Data Governance
course.description: How raw data becomes trusted analysis: dimensional models, transformation layers, tests and metrics, then lineage, quality, privacy and the roles that govern all of it.
course.audience: A capable adult who can write SQL joins and aggregates (sql-from-rows-to-reports) and has seen a data pipeline (data-engineering helps but is not required). No previous modelling or governance knowledge assumed. Tools such as dbt are named only as examples.

paragraphs: A report is only as good as the table behind it, and a table that was built without care can give a total that is too large, a history that has been rewritten or a figure that two dashboards report differently, all without any error being raised. Analytics engineering is the work of building tables so that such faults cannot arise, and of testing, measuring and documenting them so that those who read the report have reason to believe it.

The course follows one stretch of data from the question to the person who answers for it. It begins with the shape of a model, where a business question becomes a grain, facts and dimensions, and history is kept for attributes that change. It then moves to the layers of transformation, incremental builds, data tests and a semantic layer that defines a metric once. The third part traces lineage, measures quality and agrees contracts and service levels, and the last asks what the law and good practice require of anyone who holds personal data, from classification to erasure to the roles that make governance real.

Every lesson works from small tables whose answers you can check by hand, and asks you to predict what a query, a join or a test returns before it shows you the result. Tools such as dbt and OpenLineage are named as examples of how the ideas are put into practice and are not needed to follow them. The material on privacy law is educational and is not legal advice.
outcomes: You'll be able to declare a grain and design a star schema around it.
You'll be able to keep history in dimensions and avoid fan-out in joins.
You'll be able to place logic in layers, write data tests and define metrics once.
You'll be able to trace lineage, measure quality and read a contract and a service level.
You'll be able to classify and protect personal data and explain what governance has to do in practice.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on SQL: From Rows to Reports, Data Engineering: Pipelines, Warehouses and Lakehouses.

modules.title: Modelling for analysis
modules.description: Grain, facts and dimensions, slowly changing history and the trade-offs between model shapes.

modules.title: Transformation layers
modules.description: Staging, intermediate and mart models, incremental builds, tests and a semantic layer that defines metrics once.

modules.title: Lineage and quality
modules.description: Following data back to its sources, measuring quality, and agreeing contracts and service levels.

modules.title: Privacy and governance
modules.description: Classifying and protecting data, privacy law in practice and the roles that make governance real.

concepts.title: Business process
concepts.summary: A measurable activity the business performs, such as taking an order or shipping a parcel, produces the events a model records.

concepts.title: Grain
concepts.summary: The grain states exactly what one row of a fact table represents, such as one order line, and every column must be true at that grain.

concepts.title: Four design steps
concepts.summary: Dimensional design chooses the business process, declares the grain, identifies the dimensions and identifies the facts, in that order.

concepts.title: Star schema
concepts.summary: A fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive context, joined by keys.

concepts.title: Additivity
concepts.summary: Additive measures can be summed across every dimension, semi-additive ones across all but time, and non-additive ones such as ratios not at all.

concepts.title: Fact table types
concepts.summary: A transaction fact records events, a periodic snapshot records state at regular intervals, and an accumulating snapshot tracks one row through a process with several dates.

concepts.title: Surrogate key
concepts.summary: A meaningless integer key owned by the warehouse, which survives changes in source keys and allows history.

concepts.title: Degenerate dimension
concepts.summary: An identifier such as an order number kept on the fact table because it has no attributes of its own.

concepts.title: Slowly changing dimension
concepts.summary: An attribute of a dimension, such as a customer's city, changes occasionally, and the model must decide whether the past should show the old or the new value.

concepts.title: Type 1 and Type 2
concepts.summary: Type 1 overwrites the value and loses history, while Type 2 adds a new row with validity dates so history is kept.

concepts.title: As-of join
concepts.summary: A fact joins the dimension row whose validity range contains the fact's date.

concepts.title: Conformed dimensions
concepts.summary: A dimension shared by several fact tables with identical keys and meaning, so their results can be combined.

concepts.title: Normalised and dimensional
concepts.summary: A normalised model avoids redundancy for updating, a dimensional model repeats descriptions to make reading simple and fast.

concepts.title: One big table
concepts.summary: A denormalised wide table is easy to query for one purpose but repeats data and hides grain.

concepts.title: Data vault
concepts.summary: A model of hubs (keys), links (relationships) and satellites (history) built for auditable integration from many sources, usually with marts built on top.

concepts.title: Join fan-out
concepts.summary: Joining a one-to-many relationship repeats the parent row once per child, so a parent measure summed after the join is inflated.

concepts.title: Staging
concepts.summary: Staging models mirror one source table each, renaming columns, fixing types and changing nothing else.

concepts.title: Intermediate and marts
concepts.summary: Intermediate models join and reshape, and marts present business entities and measures for use.

concepts.title: Materialisation
concepts.summary: A model can be built as a view, a table, an incremental table or inlined as ephemeral, trading build time against query time and freshness.

concepts.title: Model graph
concepts.summary: Models refer to each other by reference rather than table name, so the tool builds a graph and runs models in dependency order.

concepts.title: Incremental filter
concepts.summary: An incremental run selects only rows newer than the maximum timestamp already in the target and merges them by key.

concepts.title: Lookback window
concepts.summary: Re-reading a recent window each run catches late-arriving rows, and a unique key keeps the re-read from duplicating.

concepts.title: Full refresh
concepts.summary: Rebuilding the whole model from scratch repairs logic changes and missed rows at the cost of a long build.

concepts.title: Snapshots
concepts.summary: A snapshot records how a mutable source row changes over time, adding validity dates, so history exists when the source overwrites it.

concepts.title: Tests return failing rows
concepts.summary: A data test is a query written so that it returns the rows that break the assertion, and it passes when it returns none.

concepts.title: The standard four
concepts.summary: unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships cover most structural assumptions about a column.

concepts.title: Where to test
concepts.summary: Test sources for what you receive, staging for keys, and marts for business rules, because a failure is cheapest to explain closest to its cause.

concepts.title: Unit tests and data tests
concepts.summary: A data test checks real data after a build, while a unit test checks the transformation logic against small fixed inputs.

concepts.title: Metric
concepts.summary: A named calculation, such as revenue or average order value, with an agreed definition, grain and filters.

concepts.title: Semantic layer
concepts.summary: A layer that defines metrics and dimensions once, so every dashboard and query returns the same number.

concepts.title: Metric types
concepts.summary: Simple metrics aggregate a measure, ratio metrics divide two metrics, cumulative metrics accumulate over time and derived metrics combine metrics.

concepts.title: Non-additive metrics
concepts.summary: Distinct counts and ratios cannot be added across groups, and must be recomputed at the requested grain.

concepts.title: Lineage
concepts.summary: A record of which datasets and jobs produced which other datasets, so data can be traced back to sources and forward to uses.

concepts.title: Upstream and downstream
concepts.summary: Upstream nodes feed a dataset, and downstream nodes consume it, directly or through other nodes.

concepts.title: Impact analysis
concepts.summary: Walking downstream from a changing node lists the models, reports and owners that a change can break.

concepts.title: Lineage events
concepts.summary: Jobs can emit run events naming their input and output datasets, and a lineage store assembles them into a graph.

concepts.title: Quality dimensions
concepts.summary: Completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency and timeliness name different ways data can be wrong.

concepts.title: Quality as a rate
concepts.summary: Each dimension becomes a rate, such as non-null rows over all rows, compared with a threshold agreed with the data's users.

concepts.title: Volume anomalies
concepts.summary: A z-score, the distance from the recent mean in standard deviations, flags a day whose row count is unusual.

concepts.title: Freshness target
concepts.summary: Timeliness is measured as age against a target, and a breach is the amount by which the age exceeds it.

concepts.title: Data contract
concepts.summary: An agreement between a producer and its consumers on schema, meaning, quality and timeliness of a dataset, checked automatically.

concepts.title: Breaking change
concepts.summary: Removing, renaming or retyping a field, or changing its meaning, breaks consumers, while adding an optional field does not.

concepts.title: Service-level objective
concepts.summary: A target for a measurable indicator, such as 99% of days with data ready by 07:00, over a set period.

concepts.title: Error budget
concepts.summary: The allowed failure implied by the objective, such as 1% of a 30-day month, which is 7.2 hours.

concepts.title: Classification
concepts.summary: Data is labelled by sensitivity, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, and the label drives who can see it and how it is stored.

concepts.title: Personal data
concepts.summary: Any information relating to an identifiable person, including indirect identifiers such as a postcode and age together.

concepts.title: Pseudonymisation and anonymisation
concepts.summary: Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers but can be reversed or guessed and remains personal data, while true anonymisation cannot be linked back to a person.

concepts.title: k-anonymity
concepts.summary: A table has k-anonymity when every combination of quasi-identifiers appears at least k times, so no row is unique among its group.

concepts.title: Principles
concepts.summary: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, for specified purposes, minimally, accurately, for no longer than needed, and securely, with the controller accountable.

concepts.title: Lawful bases
concepts.summary: There are six lawful bases for processing: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.

concepts.title: Data subject rights
concepts.summary: People may access their data, correct it, have it erased in some cases, restrict or object to processing, and receive it in a portable format.

concepts.title: Erasure in immutable storage
concepts.summary: Deleting a row in a table format writes a new version, and the old files remain on storage until they are vacuumed.

concepts.title: Governance roles
concepts.summary: The owner is accountable for a dataset, the steward maintains its definitions and quality, and the custodian runs the platform that stores it.

concepts.title: Catalogue and glossary
concepts.summary: A catalogue records technical, business and operational metadata for datasets, and a glossary fixes the meaning of business terms.

concepts.title: From policy to control
concepts.summary: A policy becomes a rule the platform enforces, such as a masking rule on a classified column or a retention job, rather than a document to remember.

concepts.title: Certified datasets
concepts.summary: A dataset marked as reviewed, owned and monitored tells consumers which sources to trust.

lessons.title: From questions to grain

steps.headline: A business question points at an activity, and that activity, the business process, produces the rows a model records.

lead.text: Take the question *what share of orders ship late?* It mentions no table and no column. It mentions an activity, the packing and shipping of orders, and an activity that a business performs repeatedly, and whose every occurrence can be dated and measured, is called a **business process**. Each time the process happens it leaves a record of when, of what and of how much, and those records, not the tables that the software happens to use, are what a model for analysis is built from.

Processes are named for the activity: taking an order, shipping an order, handling a return. The name matters because it tells you which measurements to expect. Order taking leaves behind quantities and prices, whereas **order fulfilment**, the work of packing and shipping what was ordered, leaves behind a promised date and a shipped date, and only fulfilment can say whether a parcel was late.

It is tempting to begin from the columns that already exist in the order system and ask what questions they allow, but the order runs the other way. *The question picks the process*, the process decides which measurements are worth bringing in, and the columns follow.

Suppose a table has one row for each order line. Order 1001 has two lines, of 20.00 and 30.00, and carries a shipping fee of 5.00. To make each row show everything about its order, the fee is copied onto both rows.

reveal.text: The column adds up to 10.00, although the customer paid the fee only once, and the next screen explains where the extra 5.00 comes from.

steps.headline: The grain says exactly what one row stands for, and every column in the table must be true at that grain.

lead.text: The excess in the last screen came from a table whose rows did not stand for one definite thing: each row was a line, yet one of its columns described the whole order. Dimensional design prevents this by stating, before any column is chosen, the **grain** of the fact table, a single sentence that says what one row represents. *One row per order line* is a grain, and once it is declared the figure shows which columns can be filled in honestly: the quantity, the unit price and the line amount each belong to one line, so each is **true at this grain**.

afterFigure.text: The shipping fee is not. It is charged once per order, so it is true at *order* grain, and putting it on a line row asks the row to say something about a thing it does not stand for. A good grain statement is also concrete: "sales" or "daily sales data" do not say what a row is, whereas "one row per product on each receipt line" does, and only the second tells you what a count of rows would mean.

The grain can fail in the other direction as well. One row per individual unit shipped would need a record that the warehouse never wrote, and since a table can always be summed up to something coarser but never split into rows that were not recorded, the grain should be as fine as the questions require and no finer than the data supports.

diagram.alt: Two views of a table design. With the grain one row per order line, quantity, unit price and line amount are true and the order shipping fee is not. With the grain one row per order, order date, shipping fee and order total are true and the quantity of one product is not.
diagram.caption: The grain decides which columns are true. Use the buttons to change the grain.

lead.text: The grain is now declared as one row per order line. Look at the columns that could go in the table.

reveal.text: A column that describes the whole order has to live in a table whose rows are orders, or be shared out between lines by a rule that is written down.

steps.headline: A column that is true at a coarser grain repeats on every row, so adding it up counts it once per row.

lead.text: A table whose rows are lines but which also carries an order_total column has **mixed grain**: some of its columns describe the line and one describes the order. The mixing stays invisible until someone adds the column up. Take three orders of 80, 120 and 250, with three, one and two lines. Each line row repeats its order's total, so 80 appears three times, 120 once and 250 twice, and SUM(order_total) is 80 × 3 + 120 × 1 + 250 × 2, which is 860, although the three orders came to 450 in all.

afterFigure.text: The query is correct and the data is in the table, which is why the fault is hard to find: nothing fails, the figure is merely too large, and it is too large by a different factor for every order, so no single correction repairs it. The cure is the one from the last screen. Keep order-level amounts in a table of orders, or leave them off the line table, so that *every* column is true at its grain and a sum of an amount column means what it says.

steps.headline: Find how much SUM(order_total) overstates revenue when orders of 60, 90 and 30 have 2, 3 and 1 lines.

workedSteps.text: Write down what each order contributes to the line table: its total, once for every line it has.
Work out each product.
SUM adds all the rows, which is the total of those three products.
The orders themselves came to the sum of the three totals.
The overstatement is the difference between the two.

steps.headline: Now find the sum for orders of 50, 70 and 90 with 2, 4 and 1 lines.

workedSteps.text: Each total is added once for every line it has.
The three products are 100, 280 and 90, and the table sums them.
Work out what SUM(order_total) returns over the line table.

steps.headline: Four decisions, taken in order, produce a star: a fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of context.

lead.text: Dimensional design is a sequence of four decisions, and the order is the point. First **choose the business process**, then **declare the grain**, then **identify the dimensions**, the descriptive context, such as who, what, where and when, that every row can be attached to, and only then **identify the facts**, the numeric measurements that are true at the grain. Settling the grain before the columns is what keeps the quantity and the line amount in the table and the shipping fee out of it.

afterFigure.text: Drawn out, the result has a fact table in the middle with one [[foreign key|A column whose values point at the key of a row in another table. Met in the SQL course.]] to each dimension, which looks like a star and is called a **star schema**. For retail sales with the grain one row per product on each receipt line, the dimensions are date, store, product and customer, and each fact row points at exactly one row in each. A question such as sales by store by month then becomes a join from the fact table to two dimensions followed by a GROUP BY, which is SQL you already know.

diagram.alt: A star schema for retail sales. A banner states the grain. In the first view only the fact table is shown. In the second four dimension tables, date, store, product and customer, surround it with arrows. In the third the fact table lists quantity, unit price and line amount.

reveal.text: The fact table is little more than its measurements and its keys, and it is the dimensions that hold the names, addresses and descriptions.

lead.text: A shipping fee of 5.00 is charged once per order, and a careless design copies it onto every line row. Order 1 has 4 lines and order 2 has 1 line.

reveal.text: Declaring the grain first would have placed the fee in a table with one row per order, where the sum is exactly 10.00.

lessons.orientation: Turn a question into a business process and a declared grain, and spot a table whose grain is mixed.
lessons.nextAction: Classify measures by how they can be added, and choose between three kinds of fact table.

blocks.text: "What share of orders ship late?" is a question about one activity, the packing and shipping of orders, and every number needed to answer it was written down at the moment that activity happened: when the order was placed, when delivery was promised and when the parcel left the warehouse.

A dimensional model starts from a question of this kind and works backwards to a table whose rows are exactly those moments. The decisions that fix the table, above all what one row stands for, matter more than any column in it, because when they are right the later queries are plain sums and when they are wrong the sums come out too large without any error being reported.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn a business question into a process and a declared grain, and to recognise a fact table whose grain is mixed.
intro.whyItMatters: A wrong grain produces totals that look right and are not.

recap.keyIdea: A fact table is declared at one grain, a sentence saying what one row stands for, and every column must be true at that grain.

blocks.text: You started from a question, found the business process behind it and declared a grain for the table that records it. You saw that a column belonging to a coarser grain, such as an order total on a line table, repeats on every row and inflates any sum, which is why the grain is settled before the columns.
The four steps, which are process, grain, dimensions and facts, give a fact table surrounded by dimensions, the star schema.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the facts themselves, and at which of them can safely be added up.

lessons.title: Facts and dimensions

lead.text: A warehouse records the stock of product P1 at the close of each day.

reveal.text: 125 units were never on the shelves at once. The three figures count mostly the same units on three evenings, and the next screens say which measures can be added at all.

steps.headline: A measure can be summed across every dimension, across all but time, or across none, and which it is decides how it may be aggregated.

lead.text: The reason 125 is the wrong answer is that stock is a *level*, while quantity sold is an *amount of activity*. Quantity sold is **additive**, which means it can be summed across every dimension of the fact table, whether days, stores or products, and still give something real. A stock level is **semi-additive**: it can be summed across products on a single day, which gives the units in the warehouse that night, but not across days, because Tuesday's units are largely Monday's again. Over time you take the end-of-period value or an average instead.

The third kind is the **non-additive** measure, which cannot be summed across any dimension, and the usual examples are ratios such as a margin percentage or a unit price. The figure lets you try each aggregation on the same small table of stock.

afterFigure.text: The sum across products on Wednesday, 65 units, is a real quantity, and so are the last value, 50, and the average, 41.67. Only the sum across days is meaningless. A fact table is therefore designed with the measure's kind in mind, so that the queries written against it use the aggregation that matches.

diagram.alt: A table of daily stock for products P1 and P2 over Monday to Wednesday. Four views highlight different ways of combining it: adding the two products for Wednesday gives 65, adding the three days for P1 gives 125 which is not meaningful, the last value for P1 is 50, and the average for P1 is 41.67.

lead.text: Think about what a margin percentage is made of.

reveal.text: A ratio has a different denominator on every row, so adding or averaging the percentages ignores how large each row is.

steps.headline: A non-additive measure is stored as its additive parts and divided only at the end.

lead.text: Suppose one sales line has revenue 200 and cost 150, a margin of 25%, and another has revenue 800 and cost 400, a margin of 50%. Averaging the two percentages gives 37.5%, which treats a line of 200 as equal in weight to a line of 800. The margin of the two lines together is the total profit over the total revenue, (1,000 − 550) / 1,000, which is 45%.

The rule that follows is to store **additive parts** in the fact table, here revenue and cost, sum them over whatever rows the question covers, and divide *last*. Unit price follows the same rule, since total revenue divided by total quantity is the price that the whole set of sales actually achieved, and it will not equal the average of the individual prices unless every line sold the same quantity.

steps.headline: Find the margin of two sales lines, one with revenue 200 and cost 150, the other with revenue 800 and cost 400.

workedSteps.text: Work out each line's margin first, to see what an average of them would give.
Averaging the two percentages gives 37.5%, but that is not the margin of the lines together.
Add the additive parts instead: total revenue and total cost.
Divide only now, profit over revenue.

steps.headline: Find the average unit price of two sales lines, 10 units for 300 and 5 units for 100.

workedSteps.text: Sum the additive parts: total revenue and total quantity.
Divide revenue by quantity last, as the price the whole set achieved.

steps.headline: A transaction fact records events, a periodic snapshot records state at regular intervals, and an accumulating snapshot follows one row through a process.

lead.text: The stock table and the sales table have different grains, and the difference is a design choice that has a name. A **transaction fact** table adds one row whenever something happens, such as a sale line, and the row is not changed afterwards. A **periodic snapshot** adds a row for every item in every period, such as one row per product per day, whether or not anything happened, which is what makes a level like stock readable. An **accumulating snapshot** has one row per instance of a process, such as one order, with a column for the date of each milestone, and the row is updated as each milestone is reached.

afterFigure.text: Order A7 in the figure has been ordered, paid and shipped, so its delivery date is still blank, and it will be filled in later, whereas a transaction row would never be revisited. The accumulating snapshot suits questions about the time between milestones, for instance days from payment to delivery. The three kinds often sit side by side for the same business.

lead.text: A retailer wants to read the stock of every product on every day, including days when nothing was sold.

reveal.text: A table that only records events cannot show a product that did nothing, which is why stock is kept as snapshots.

steps.headline: A surrogate key is a meaningless integer owned by the warehouse, so a dimension never depends on a source system's ids.

lead.text: A dimension row has to be identified by something, and the tempting choice is the id that the source system uses, called the *business key*. The figure shows the difficulty: two systems each number their customers from their own list, so id 17 is Ada in one and Cy in the other, and a join on the id alone would attach Cy's sales to Ada. A source may also change an id, or reuse one, and a key that follows the source loses the history of the row.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is a **surrogate key**, an integer without meaning that the warehouse itself assigns to each dimension row, such as customer_key, kept beside the source id as an ordinary attribute. Fact rows point at the surrogate key, and the next lesson shows how it also lets a dimension keep several versions of one customer. Some identifiers do not need a dimension of their own: an order number that has no attributes beyond itself is simply kept on the fact table as a **degenerate dimension**, and is used to group lines back into orders.

lessons.orientation: Classify measures by how they add, pick a fact table type, and see why dimensions use surrogate keys.
lessons.nextAction: Keep history in a dimension and join each fact to the version that was true on its date.

blocks.text: The stock of one product closes at 40 units on Monday, 35 on Tuesday and 50 on Wednesday. Units sold, by contrast, are new each day: 8, 12 and 5 add up to 25 sold over the three days, and nobody would doubt it. A column of stock levels looks just like a column of sales, yet the same SUM over days that works for the one gives nonsense for the other.

The facts of a model are its numbers, and a model is only useful if the numbers can be aggregated safely. This lesson sorts measures by how they may be added, then looks at the three shapes a fact table can take and at the keys that tie facts to their dimensions.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how each measure may be aggregated, pick a fact table type for a process, and explain why dimensions carry a surrogate key.
intro.whyItMatters: Summing the wrong measure is one of the commonest silent errors in reports.

recap.keyIdea: A measure is additive, semi-additive or non-additive depending on whether it can be summed across every dimension, all but time, or none.

blocks.text: You sorted measures by how they add: quantity sold sums everywhere, a stock level or balance sums across products but not across days, and a ratio is rebuilt from additive parts and divided last. You also saw three kinds of fact table, transaction, periodic snapshot and accumulating snapshot, each with its own grain.
Dimensions are tied to facts by a surrogate key that the warehouse owns, because source ids can clash, change or lose history.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses that surrogate key to keep several versions of one customer, so that old sales stay attached to the facts as they were.

lessons.title: History in dimensions

lead.text: A sales representative moves from the North to the South on 1 March. Their earlier sales stay in the fact table, and a data engineer simply updates the region on the representative's dimension row.

reveal.text: The report now shows 30 for the North, though the region made 130 that quarter. The sales happened, but the dimension no longer says where.

steps.headline: A dimension attribute that changes slowly can be overwritten, which loses the past, or versioned with a new row, which keeps it.

lead.text: A representative's region, a customer's city or a product's brand changes rarely, but when it does, every question about the past is affected. Dimensions with attributes of this kind are called **slowly changing dimensions**, and the design question is what the old rows of the fact table should say after a change. The simplest answer, called **Type 1**, overwrites the attribute, so that the table holds only the current value and every old fact is reported under it, as the first screen showed.

The answer that keeps history, called **Type 2**, leaves the old row alone and adds a *new row* for the new value, with its own surrogate key. Each row also carries **validity dates**, a valid_from and a valid_to, which say between which dates the row described the representative. Two rows now stand for one person, which is why the surrogate key from the last lesson matters: the fact must point at the version, not at the person.

afterFigure.text: Neither type is better in general. Overwriting suits a correction, such as a mistyped phone number that nobody wants to see again, while versioning suits a change that really happened and that past facts should remember.

diagram.alt: Two versions of a dim_rep table after rep R1 moves from North to South. Under Type 1 the R1 row is overwritten and says South. Under Type 2 there are two R1 rows, North from 2025-01-01 to 2026-03-01 and South from 2026-03-01 to 9999-12-31.

lead.text: Think about how a Type 2 design holds R1, who was in the North until 1 March and is in the South afterwards.

reveal.text: Each row is one version, so the number of rows for a person is the number of values they have had.

steps.headline: Each version holds for a range of dates that includes its start and excludes its end, so the ranges of one person never overlap.

lead.text: A validity range has to be stated exactly, because a sale made on the very day of a change must match one row, not two. The convention used here is **half-open**: valid_from is *included* and valid_to is *excluded*. The North row of R1 runs from 2025-01-01 to 2026-03-01, which means that it holds up to, but not including, 1 March, and the South row starts on 1 March and includes it.

The row that is still true has no end yet, so it is given a far-future date such as 9999-12-31 in place of a missing value, which keeps the test for any row the same two comparisons. Some designs write the last day of each range as the end date and include it; the figure shows what then happens on the change date.

afterFigure.text: With the end date included, a sale on 1 March satisfies the test for both rows, and an as-of join would count it twice, once under each region. Excluding the end date, so that one range finishes where the next begins, rules this out.

diagram.alt: A timeline from mid February to mid March with a North bar ending on 1 March and a South bar starting on 1 March. Two sale dates, 28 February and 1 March, are marked. In the first view the end date is excluded so 1 March matches only the South row. In the second the end date is included and 1 March matches both rows.

lead.text: Consider R1's two rows, the North row ending on 2026-03-01 and the South row starting on it, with the end date excluded.

reveal.text: A date on the boundary belongs to the version that starts there, which is why a table built this way never matches twice.

steps.headline: An as-of join matches each fact to the dimension row whose validity range contains the fact's date.

lead.text: To report the sales by region as it was at the time, the fact table has to be joined to the dimension on two conditions: the same representative, and a sale date that falls in the row's range, so valid_from is at most the sale date and the sale date is before valid_to. This is an **as-of join**, and the query in the first view of the figure does exactly that. It gives the North 130 and the South 25, because the sales of 40 and 60 find the North row and the sale of 25 finds the South row.

afterFigure.text: The second view joins only to the row that is still current, which is what happens when history is forgotten. Every sale of R1 is then reported under the South, so the North shows 30 and the South 125. The same total of 155 is split differently, and nothing in the query reports an error. In practice the as-of join is often done once, when the fact table is loaded, and the fact row then stores the surrogate key of the version it matched, so that later queries need only an ordinary join on that key.

queries.label: As-of join (valid on the sale date)
queries.sql: SELECT d.region, SUM(s.amount) AS total FROM sales s JOIN dim_rep d ON d.rep_id = s.rep_id AND s.sale_date >= d.valid_from AND s.sale_date < d.valid_to GROUP BY d.region ORDER BY d.region;

queries.label: Current row only
queries.sql: SELECT d.region, SUM(s.amount) AS total FROM sales s JOIN dim_rep d ON d.rep_id = s.rep_id AND d.valid_to = '9999-12-31' GROUP BY d.region ORDER BY d.region;

The sale of 60 on 2026-02-14 is also before the change date. The sale of 25 on 2026-04-05 is after it.

steps.headline: Versioning has other forms, and a dimension shared by several facts must keep the same keys and meaning in all of them.

lead.text: Type 1 and Type 2 are the two forms that matter most, and the others can be put in a line each. **Type 0** never changes an attribute once it has been loaded. **Type 3** adds a column for the previous value, so that one step of history is kept without a new row. **Type 6**, a hybrid, combines the first, second and third by adding a row for each version and also carrying the current value on every row. Tools build the versions for you, and dbt's snapshots, which a later lesson returns to, record each change as a new row with validity dates in the same way.

Once a dimension keeps history, it is worth sharing. A sales fact table and a returns fact table that both join to the same product dimension, with identical keys and meaning, use a **conformed dimension**, and the benefit is that their results can be put side by side: sales and returns by product can be compared because both mean the same thing by product.
Consider a business with one fact table for sales and another for returns, both pointing to the same product dimension.

reveal.text: If the two facts used different product tables, the same product could appear under two names, and a comparison of sales and returns would not line up.

lead.text: A customer's phone number was typed wrongly at sign-up and has now been corrected in the source system. No report has ever used the number to group sales.

reveal.text: Not every change deserves a new row. A new version is worth its cost only when past facts should still show the old value.

lessons.orientation: Choose between overwriting and versioning a dimension attribute, and join facts to the row valid on their date.
lessons.nextAction: Compare dimensional models with other shapes, and detect the fan-out that makes joined totals too large.

blocks.text: On 1 March 2026 a sales representative, R1, moves from the North region to the South. Her sales of 40 in January and 60 in February were made in the North, and a report on the first quarter, run in April, ought to credit them there. Whether it does depends on a decision made long before, when the dimension table was designed: what happens to a row of a dimension when one of its attributes changes.
The fact table cannot answer this by itself, since it holds only a key and a measure. The answer lies in how the dimension keeps, or fails to keep, the version that was true when each sale happened.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between overwriting and versioning an attribute, and to join each fact to the dimension row that was true on its date.
intro.whyItMatters: Overwriting an attribute quietly rewrites every past report that uses it.

recap.keyIdea: A Type 2 dimension keeps each version of a row with validity dates, and an as-of join sends each fact to the version valid on its date.

blocks.text: You compared overwriting an attribute, Type 1, with adding a row for each version, Type 2, and saw that overwriting moves past sales to the present value while versioning keeps them where they were made. Each version carries a half-open validity range, so a sale on the day of a change matches exactly one row.
An as-of join matches a fact to the row whose range contains its date, and a dimension shared by several fact tables with the same keys is conformed.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson steps back and asks which overall shape a model should take, and why a join between two facts can silently multiply rows.

lessons.title: Choosing a model shape

lead.text: A finance team joins invoices to their lines, intending to add up the invoice totals. Invoice 1 has total 90 and 3 lines, invoice 2 has total 150 and 2 lines, and invoice 3 has total 40 and 1 line.

reveal.text: The query reports 610 when the invoices came to 280, and no error appears, because the join is correct and the total is the one that was asked for.

steps.headline: Joining a parent to its children repeats the parent once per child, so a parent measure summed after the join is inflated.

lead.text: The first lesson showed that a column true at a coarser grain repeats on every row of a finer table. A join can produce the same effect at query time, without any such column being stored. Each invoice has *one* total but several lines, so a join of invoices to lines returns one row per line, and the invoice's total is copied onto each of them. Summing it then adds the total once for every line, which is the **fan-out**: the rows multiply on the many side, and every parent measure multiplies with them.
The figure runs three queries on the same two tables. The first, which sums the invoice total after the join, returns the inflated figure. The others show ways to get the right one.

afterFigure.text: The warning sign is a row count: the join of three invoices returned six rows, more than the parent table has. A one-to-many join does that on purpose, and nothing is wrong with it as long as the measures summed belong to the *line* grain, as the line amounts do. The fault comes only from summing a measure that belongs to the parent.

queries.label: Sum the total after the join
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(i.total) AS total FROM invoices i JOIN invoice_lines l ON l.invoice_id = i.id;

queries.label: Sum on invoices alone
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(total) AS total FROM invoices;

queries.label: Aggregate lines first
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(i.total) AS total FROM invoices i JOIN (SELECT invoice_id, COUNT(*) AS line_count FROM invoice_lines GROUP BY invoice_id) l ON l.invoice_id = i.id;

lead.text: Look at the join of the three invoices to their lines, with 3, 2 and 1 lines.

reveal.text: A row count that exceeds the parent table is the simplest test for fan-out, and it costs one extra query.

steps.headline: Two repairs avoid fan-out: sum the measure at the grain it belongs to, or aggregate the many side to the parent's grain before joining.

lead.text: There are two ways out, and both work by making the sum happen at the right grain. The first is to sum the measure where it lives: invoice totals are summed over the invoices table alone, and line amounts are summed over the lines, so neither is ever joined to the other first. The second is to **aggregate the many side first**, grouping the lines to one row per invoice in a subquery and joining that to the invoices, so that each invoice matches exactly one row and cannot be repeated. This is the third query in the figure, and it returns the 280 of the invoices.

A check worth writing into any such query compares the row count, or COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT id), before and after the join, because an increase tells you at once that the parent has been repeated. In a dimensional model the check is rarely needed, since facts are joined only to dimensions, which are one-to-one with the fact row, but it matters whenever two fact tables or a parent and its children are joined.

steps.headline: Sum the totals of invoices 1, 2 and 3 (90, 150 and 40) by aggregating the lines to one row per invoice before the join.

workedSteps.text: Group the lines by invoice, so that the many side has one row for each invoice.
Join the invoices to that result on the invoice id. Each invoice now matches exactly one row.
Sum the invoice total over the three joined rows.

steps.headline: Orders 1, 2 and 3 have totals of 80, 120 and 50, with 2, 1 and 4 payments. Aggregate the payments first, then sum the totals.

workedSteps.text: Without aggregating, each total repeats once per payment, which would give 480.
Group the payments to one row per order and join that result, so each order matches once.
Work out SUM(total) over the three joined rows.

steps.headline: A normalised model, a star and a wide table hold the same facts, and each makes a different job easy.

lead.text: Fan-out is a symptom of a deeper choice: the shape in which the data is stored. A **normalised** model stores each fact once, so that a customer's address, for instance, sits in one row and can be corrected in one place, which is what an application that takes orders needs. Reading it for analysis means chaining joins across many tables, and every join is a place for a fan-out. A **dimensional** model, the star, repeats descriptions in its dimensions on purpose, so that a report groups by any attribute with a single join each. A **wide table** goes further and puts every column on every row, which means no joins at all.

afterFigure.text: The wide table is convenient for one purpose, such as feeding one tool, but it repeats data and hides the grain, since nothing says what one row is, and a second purpose usually needs a second wide table. No shape is best everywhere. The three differ in what they make easy, and a team picks the one that matches the job in front of it.

diagram.alt: Three shapes for the same retail data. A normalised model is a chain of small tables, customers, orders, order lines, products and categories. A star has one order-lines fact table with four dimensions. A wide table puts every column on one row, repeating customer, city and category.

lead.text: Choose the shape for a flat table that feeds one modelling tool and needs no joins at query time.

reveal.text: The right shape depends on the job, and a table built for one tool is a different job from a store for the order application.

steps.headline: A data vault integrates many sources with full history, and dimensional marts built on top of it serve the reports.

lead.text: A third kind of model solves a different problem, which is bringing data from many source systems into one place without losing track of where each value came from. A **data vault** splits a business into three kinds of table. A *hub* holds only the business keys of one kind of thing, such as customer or product. A *link* records a relationship between hubs, such as an order line between a customer and a product. A *satellite* hangs off a hub or link and holds its descriptive attributes with the date they were loaded, so every change is kept.

afterFigure.text: The vault is built for integration and audit rather than for reading, and it needs more tables than the star built from it. Reports are therefore served by dimensional marts on top, and a wide table may follow at the end for one tool. The three needs of integration, history and reporting differ, which is why a warehouse often uses more than one shape in layers, and why adding a table to a model is never free: each new table adds joins and ways to be wrong.

diagram.alt: Two views of a data vault. First, a layered picture: source systems feed a data vault for integration, which feeds star marts and then a wide table. Second, the inside of a vault: hubs for customer and product, a link for order line between them, and a satellite under each hub.

lead.text: Fan-out does not only inflate money. Customer 1 has a credit limit of 500 and 3 orders, and customer 2 has a limit of 800 and 2 orders.

lessons.nextAction: Place transformation logic into staging, intermediate and mart layers and choose how each model is built.

blocks.text: A join between invoices and invoice lines is the most ordinary query in an invoicing system, and it is also one of the easiest ways to make a total wrong without any error. The join is correct, and the sum is correct, but the invoice total has been copied onto each of its lines, so it is added once per line.

The same data can be stored in several shapes, and the choice of shape decides how often a query meets this trap. This lesson looks at the fan-out first, because it is the thing that goes wrong, and then at the shapes: normalised, dimensional, wide and data vault.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to detect and fix a join fan-out, and to choose between a normalised model, a star, a wide table and a data vault for a given job.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong shape, or joining carelessly, changes totals without any warning.

recap.keyIdea: Joining a parent to its children repeats the parent once per child, so measures are summed at the grain they belong to, and each shape of model suits a different job.

blocks.text: A one-to-many join returns one row per child and copies the parent's columns onto each, so summing a parent measure afterwards counts it once per child. The cure is to sum the measure at its own grain, or to aggregate the many side to one row per parent before joining, and a rising row count is the signal to look for.
A normalised model suits an application, a star suits reporting, a wide table suits a single tool and a data vault suits integration with history, so a warehouse often layers them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson begins the transformation module, and shows how those layers are organised in practice as staging, intermediate and mart models.

lessons.title: Layers of models

lead.text: A team has seven models that read the table raw.orders. Each one names the table directly, and each renames the columns in its own way.

reveal.text: Seven edits, and no guarantee that the seven new names agree. A layer that stands between the source and everything else turns this into a single change.

steps.headline: Models are arranged in layers, from staging that mirrors a source, through intermediate models that reshape, to marts that serve users.

lead.text: The figure follows one order through four models. The first layer, **staging**, has one model for each source table, and it does the dull work only: it renames orderid to order_id, casts the amount from the text "40.00" to a number, and changes nothing else. It is kept dull on purpose, because every other model reads the staging model and not the source, so a source that changes, or a column that needs cleaning, is fixed in one place and every model after it sees the same result.

The second layer is **intermediate**, where the real shaping happens: joining orders to customers, say, or reducing payments to one row per order. These models are steps on the way and are rarely shown to a user. The last layer is the **marts**, the finished tables that reports and people read, such as an orders fact table or a daily revenue table, each presenting a business entity or a set of measures.

afterFigure.text: The layers give logic a home. Renames and casts go in staging, joins and reshaping in intermediate models, and business measures in marts. Putting a join into a staging model, or a cast into a mart, is the commonest way for a project to lose this order, since each model then has to be read in full to know what it does.

In staging the columns are renamed order_id and customer_id and the amount is a number. In the intermediate model the customer name Ada is joined on. In the mart the order has a customer key.

lead.text: Here is a model that joins two staging models and keeps one row per order.

reveal.text: The question to ask of any model is how much it changes: a rename and a cast belong in staging, a join belongs further on.

steps.headline: A model can be built as a view, a table, an incremental table or inlined as ephemeral, and each trades build time against read time.

lead.text: Every model is a query, and the tool needs to be told what to do with its result, which is called the model's **materialisation**. A **view** stores nothing and runs the query again whenever it is read, so it costs nothing to build and pays each time it is read. A **table** stores the result, so reading it is fast, and it is rebuilt in full on every run. An **incremental** table keeps what it has and adds only the new rows on each run, and an **ephemeral** model is never stored at all, its query being pasted into the models that use it. In dbt the default is a view.

Choosing among them is a matter of size and use. A small lookup is cheap to recompute and suits a view. A large table that is read often suits a stored table, and one that is also large and grows by appending suits an incremental one, because the cost of a run then follows the amount of new data and not the size of the table.

diagram.alt: A table comparing four ways to materialise a model. A view builds nothing and runs its query on every read. A table is rebuilt in full each run and read quickly. An incremental table adds only new rows and is read quickly. An ephemeral model is built never and its query is inlined into the models that use it.
diagram.caption: Each kind trades build time against read time.

lead.text: An event model has 2,000,000,000 rows and gains 5,000,000 new rows every hour. Compare rebuilding it in full with adding only the new rows.

reveal.text: That ratio is the reason incremental models exist, and the next lesson shows how to build one without missing rows.

steps.headline: Models refer to each other by name rather than by table, so the tool can build a graph and run the models in dependency order.

lead.text: A model that reads another could simply name its table, in the form schema.table, but then the tool cannot tell that one depends on the other, and the order of building has to be kept by hand. In dbt a model instead calls ref('stg_orders'), and the tool reads every such call to find the dependencies. The result is a **model graph**, a set of models joined by arrows from each model to the ones that read it, with no cycles, which is why it is also called a directed acyclic graph. The tool builds models in rounds, running together all those whose parents are finished.

The figure shows eight models between three sources and a report. A reference is also what makes the names portable: the same model can build into a development schema and a production schema without being edited, because the tool fills in the real table name.

afterFigure.text: Reading the graph answers two questions at once: what must run before a given model, found by following the arrows back, and what is affected by a change in a model, found by following them forward. Switch to the build order view to see the rounds.

diagram.alt: A graph of eleven boxes. Three raw sources each feed a staging model, stg_customers, stg_orders and stg_payments. Two intermediate models, int_orders_joined and int_payments_by_order, join them. The marts are dim_customers, fct_orders and rpt_daily_revenue, with arrows between them. The views label the layers, the way each model is materialised, and the round in which each model is built.

blocks.text: A project that starts with one query tends to end with a hundred, and the trouble is rarely any one of them. It is that the hundred each rename the same columns in their own way, each join the same two tables, and each rebuild at their own time, so that nobody can say which depends on which.

Analytics engineering handles this by giving every kind of work a layer and every model a declared place in a graph. This lesson takes the layers, then the choice of how each model is built, and then the graph that lets a tool run it all in the right order.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a transformation in the right layer, choose how a model is materialised, and read a model graph for build order.
intro.whyItMatters: Layers keep a change to one source from becoming a change to every model.

recap.keyIdea: Staging, intermediate and mart layers give each transformation a place, and models that refer to each other by name let a tool build the graph and run it in order.

blocks.text: Staging models mirror one source and only rename and retype, intermediate models join and reshape, and marts present the finished entities and measures. Each model is built as a view, a table, an incremental table or an ephemeral model, which trades build time against read time.
Because models refer to each other by name, the tool can read the graph, run the models in rounds and tell you what a change will touch.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how an incremental model decides which rows are new, and how it can miss late ones.

lessons.title: Incremental builds

lead.text: An incremental model keeps what it has already built and reads only the rows that are newer than the latest updated_at in its target.

reveal.text: The run reads three of the six rows and skips three. That is the saving, and the next screens show what it costs.

steps.headline: An incremental run reads only the rows later than the latest timestamp already in the target, and merges them by key.

lead.text: The previous lesson called a model incremental when it adds to its table instead of rebuilding it. To do that it needs a rule for which source rows are new. The usual rule is a filter on a timestamp: read the rows whose updated_at is later than the *maximum* updated_at already in the target. In dbt this is written as a condition inside an is_incremental block, comparing against the existing table, and the model also declares a **unique key**. The rows read are then merged into the target by that key, so that a changed row replaces its old version and a new row is added.

The figure puts six source rows on a time axis. The target's latest timestamp is 10 June, so the dashed line sits there, and the rows to its right, ids 2, 5 and 6, are read. Id 2 is a change to a row that is already in the target, and ids 5 and 6 are new.

afterFigure.text: The saving is plain: three rows are read in place of six, and on a large table the proportion is far smaller. The rule rests on an assumption, though, that rows arrive in timestamp order, so that nothing older than the target's latest timestamp can turn up later. Id 4 is the counterexample, and the next screens deal with it.

In the first view a cut-off line at 10 June separates the rows read, 2, 5 and 6, from the rest, and row 4, a late row, is missed. In the second view the cut-off is 8 June and rows 2 to 6 are read.

lead.text: The run reads ids 2, 5 and 6 and merges them into the target by id.

reveal.text: The merge is by key, which is what lets an incremental model both change old rows and add new ones in a single step.

steps.headline: A row that arrives late carries an old timestamp, so the filter never reads it, and a unique key cannot rescue a row that is never read.

lead.text: Id 4 in the figure was stamped 9 June, but it reached the source only after the target had already loaded rows up to 10 June. Its timestamp is *older* than the target's latest, so the filter skips it, and it will be skipped on every later run, since the latest timestamp can only grow. The model has silently diverged from the source: a full rebuild would include id 4, and the incremental one never will.

It is tempting to think the unique key protects against this. It does not, because the key matters only to rows that have been read, in deciding whether each replaces an existing row or is added. A **late-arriving** row is one the filter has to read in the first place, so the repair has to be made in the filter.
Compare the six source rows with the three target rows and the filter's cut-off of 10 June.

reveal.text: Finding the row by hand is easy on six rows, and a check that counts rows in the source and the target does the same job on millions.

steps.headline: A lookback window re-reads recent rows on every run, and the unique key keeps the re-read from creating duplicates.

lead.text: The repair is to move the cut-off back. Instead of reading rows later than the target's latest timestamp, the run reads rows later than that timestamp *minus a few days*, which is called a **lookback window**. Rows that arrived late, but not too late, fall inside it, and rows that were already loaded are read again and merged by the unique key, so each simply replaces itself and nothing is duplicated. This is where the unique key earns its place.

The window costs something, since it re-reads rows that were already loaded, so it should be as short as the lateness allows. The figure has the queries for a one-day and a two-day window on the same tables. The two-day window reads rows 2 to 6, which includes the late row, and the one-day window reads only 2, 3, 5 and 6, because row 4 is stamped on the cut-off date itself.

afterFigure.text: The comparison with the cut-off is strict, so the window has to be longer than the longest delay by at least a day. Choosing it means finding out how late rows really arrive, and not hoping.

queries.label: Incremental filter
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, updated_at FROM src WHERE updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM tgt) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Lookback of 2 days
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, updated_at FROM src WHERE updated_at > date((SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM tgt), '-2 days') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Lookback of 1 day
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, updated_at FROM src WHERE updated_at > date((SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM tgt), '-1 days') ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Run the model with a lookback of 2 days against the six source rows, merging by id.

workedSteps.text: The target's latest updated_at is 2026-06-10, so the cut-off is two days earlier.
Read the rows later than the cut-off: every source row except id 1, which is stamped exactly 06-08.
Merge by id. Id 3 is already in the target, so it replaces itself.
Id 2 is updated, ids 4, 5 and 6 are added, and id 1 is untouched, so the target now matches the source.

steps.headline: Repeat the run with a lookback of only 1 day, and see whether id 4 is read.

workedSteps.text: The cut-off is one day before the latest timestamp.
Id 4 is stamped exactly 2026-06-09, which is not later than the cut-off, so it is left out again.
Count the source rows read: ids 2, 3, 5 and 6 are later than 06-09. How many is that?

steps.headline: A change to a model's logic does not rewrite old rows, so a full refresh rebuilds the table from scratch when the past is wrong.

lead.text: Some faults a lookback cannot reach. If the definition of a model changes, say to store amounts in cents, an incremental run applies the new logic only to the rows it reads, and every other row keeps the old one, so the table holds a mixture. A row that was missed long ago is out of the window as well. The remedy is a **full refresh**, which drops the table and rebuilds it from the whole source, and it costs the long build that incremental models exist to avoid.

A full refresh is therefore kept for repairs, and some teams schedule one regularly, say each week, as a safety net, so that any drift from late rows is cleared. The incremental model is then fast on most days and exactly right again after each refresh.
The model's amounts change to cents, and the target already holds six rows built in the old unit.

reveal.text: Because old rows are not rewritten, the table is now half in dollars and half in cents, which is worse than either, since no query can tell which is which.

steps.headline: A snapshot records how a mutable source row changes over time, so that history exists when the source overwrites it.

lead.text: All of this assumed a source whose rows stay as they were. Many sources are overwritten: when invoice 2's amount changes from 40 to 55, the source simply holds 55, and the 40 is gone for ever. A **snapshot** keeps a copy of the row each time it changes, adding validity dates, so that the old version closes at the moment the new one opens. This is the idea of a Type 2 dimension, applied to a source table. In dbt a snapshot can detect a change by comparing a timestamp such as updated_at, or by comparing the values of chosen columns, and it adds columns named dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to.
History cannot be recovered afterwards, only recorded from the moment you start, so a snapshot of a table that will be overwritten is taken early and run on a schedule.

lessons.orientation: Predict which rows an incremental run reads and misses, and choose a lookback, refresh or snapshot.
lessons.nextAction: Write tests as queries that return the failing rows, and decide where in the graph to put them.

blocks.text: An incremental model rests on a promise that sounds modest: rows that are already loaded do not change, and rows that are new have newer timestamps. When the promise holds, a run processes a few thousand rows where a full rebuild would process billions, and a table that took an hour to build takes seconds.

When it fails, nothing breaks. The model keeps running, on time and without error, while its table drifts away from the source one late row at a time. This lesson shows exactly which rows an incremental run reads, which it misses, and the three repairs: a lookback window, a full refresh and a snapshot.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict which rows an incremental model reads and which it misses, and choose a lookback or a refresh to close the gap.
intro.whyItMatters: A model that drifts from its source without an error is worse than one that fails.

recap.keyIdea: An incremental run reads only rows newer than the target's latest timestamp, so late rows and changed logic are missed unless a lookback or a full refresh repairs them.

blocks.text: An incremental filter reads rows later than the latest updated_at in the target and merges them by the unique key, which saves most of the work. A row that arrives late carries an old timestamp and is never read, and the key cannot help, so a lookback window reads a recent stretch again and lets the key stop duplicates.
A change of logic reaches old rows only through a full refresh, and a snapshot records the history of a source row that gets overwritten.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to testing, and how to write a query whose rows are the failures.

lessons.title: Testing data

lead.text: Data tests are small queries that run against real tables. One of them, unique, looks for email values that appear more than once. The employees table has seven rows, with the emails ana, bo, missing, bo, eli, fay and missing.

reveal.text: One row comes back, for bo. The two missing emails are a different fault, and testing for it is a job for a different test.

steps.headline: A data test is a query that returns the rows that break an assertion, and it passes when it returns none.

lead.text: A test could be written to answer yes or no, or to return a count of rows that pass, but a better design is to return the *failing rows themselves*. The test is then an ordinary query whose result is the evidence: it **passes** when it returns no rows, and it **fails** when it returns any, and when it fails the rows say which records broke the rule, so no second query is needed to find the cause. Tools such as dbt run this way, and so do rule-based libraries such as Great Expectations in their own form.

The first view of the figure is the **unique** test on the employees' email: it groups the non-missing emails and keeps those that appear more than once, so it returns bo with a count of two. The second is the **not_null** test, which returns the employees whose email is missing, ids 3 and 7. The third is the unique test on id, which returns nothing, and so passes.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the unique test skips missing values by design. A missing email is not a duplicate of another missing email, and treating it as one would blur two separate rules. The right habit is to write each assumption as its own test, so that a failure names the assumption that broke.

queries.label: unique test on email
queries.sql: SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

queries.label: not_null test on email
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM employees WHERE email IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: unique test on id
queries.sql: SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees GROUP BY id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

lead.text: Look at the not_null test in the figure, which returns the employees whose email is missing.

reveal.text: The test returns whole rows, so the person who reads the failure sees the ids and can look them up at the source.

steps.headline: Two more standard tests check that a column refers to a real parent row and that its values come from an allowed list.

lead.text: The **relationships** test checks that every value in a column points at a row of another table, which is the rule behind a join: an employee's dept_id should be the id of a real department. It is written by joining the child to the parent and keeping the child rows where no parent was found. Employee 6 has dept_id 99 and there is no such department, so it is returned. Employee 5 has a missing dept_id, and is *not* returned, because a value that was never given points at nothing and so breaks no reference. Whether the column may be missing is a rule of its own, which not_null states.

The **accepted_values** test checks a column against a list: employees may be active, on leave or left, and the test returns any row with another status. Employee 6 has the status retired, so it is returned. Together with unique and not_null these make up the *standard four*, which cover most of the structural assumptions that a model makes about a column.

afterFigure.text: Add retired to the list and the same test passes, as the third view shows. A test is a statement of what the team currently believes, and a failure can mean the data is wrong or the belief is out of date, which is for a person to decide.

queries.label: relationships test on dept_id
queries.sql: SELECT e.id, e.dept_id FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL AND d.id IS NULL;

queries.label: accepted_values test on status
queries.sql: SELECT id, status FROM employees WHERE status NOT IN ('active', 'leave', 'left');

queries.label: accepted_values with retired added
queries.sql: SELECT id, status FROM employees WHERE status NOT IN ('active', 'leave', 'left', 'retired');

lead.text: The employees' dept_id is checked against the departments table, which holds the ids 10, 20 and 30.

reveal.text: A relationships test reports children whose parent is not there, and it deliberately stays silent about a key that was never given.

steps.headline: Write the relationships test for employees.dept_id against departments.id, and find the failing rows.

workedSteps.text: Start from the child rows that carry a value, since a missing dept_id points at nothing and breaks no reference.
workedSteps.math: FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL

workedSteps.text: Look for the parent of each, by joining departments on the key with a LEFT JOIN, which keeps the employee even when no department matches.
workedSteps.math: LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id

workedSteps.text: Keep the rows where no parent was found, since a missing d.id means there was nothing to join to.
Run it. Employee 6 has dept_id 99, which matches no department, so one row is returned and the test fails.

steps.headline: Write the accepted_values test for the order statuses paid, paid, shipped, refunded, paid, void and paid, with only paid and shipped allowed.

workedSteps.text: Select the rows whose status is not in the list of allowed values.
Neither refunded nor void is on the list, so each such row is returned as a failure.
Count the rows the test returns.

steps.headline: Test the sources for what arrives, staging for keys and marts for business rules, because a failure is cheapest to explain closest to its cause.

lead.text: Where a test sits in the graph decides how useful its failure is. Suppose a duplicate customer id arrives from the source. A unique test on the source or staging model names it at once, with the failing row in hand. If nothing tests until the final mart, the same duplicate has been joined into several models, and has multiplied totals along the way, so the failure shows up as a wrong figure hours later, far from where it began.

A practical arrangement follows the layers. *Sources* get tests for what you receive: key columns not missing, codes from the allowed list, and data that is fresh enough. *Staging* models get the structural tests on keys, unique and not_null on the id and relationships to the parent. *Marts* get the business rules, such as revenue never being negative, since those need the joined and shaped result. The figure shows each in place.

reveal.text: The best place is the first model where the key has its final name, since every model after it inherits the same guarantee.

steps.headline: A data test checks real data after a build, while a unit test checks the transformation logic against small fixed inputs.

lead.text: Everything so far is a **data test**: it runs on the real tables after the model is built, and it tells you whether *this* data satisfies a rule. A data test cannot tell you whether the model's logic is right, because a bug and a data problem can look alike, and a test that passes on today's data may not exercise the awkward cases at all.

A **unit test** checks the logic instead. It gives the model a few input rows that you wrote, including the awkward ones, such as a negative amount or a missing key, and compares the output with the output you expect. Since the inputs are fixed, the test runs before any real data is touched and gives the same answer every time, so a failure points at the code. The two kinds therefore answer different questions: data tests ask whether the data is as assumed, and unit tests ask whether the logic does what it should.
A business rule says the ship date must not be before the order date. Four orders are ordered on 05-01, 05-04, 05-05 and 05-06 and shipped on 05-03, 05-02, 05-05 and 05-04.

reveal.text: A rule that no standard test covers is written the same way, as a query that returns the rows that break it. Such a test belongs in a mart, where both dates are present.

lessons.orientation: Write tests as failing-row queries, read the four standard tests, and place a test in the graph.
lessons.nextAction: Define a metric once in a semantic layer, and avoid double counting when it is sliced.

blocks.text: A model can build without an error and still be wrong: an id that appears twice, a status that nobody expected, an order that points at a customer who does not exist. Nothing in the build notices, because the build only runs the query.

A data test is how a team writes down such an assumption so that a machine can check it on every run. The form that works best is a query that returns the rows breaking the assumption, because an empty result then means that the assumption holds, and a non-empty one shows exactly which records to look at.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a test as a query that returns failing rows, read the four standard tests, and decide where in the graph a test belongs.
intro.whyItMatters: A test that returns the failing rows tells you what broke, not only that something did.

recap.keyIdea: A data test is a query that returns the rows breaking an assumption, so it passes when it returns none, and it belongs as close to the cause as possible.

blocks.text: The four standard tests are unique, not_null, relationships and accepted_values, and each returns the rows that break it. Missing values are the business of not_null, so unique and relationships skip them, and each assumption gets its own test.
Sources are tested for what arrives, staging models for their keys and marts for business rules, and unit tests check the logic against small fixed inputs where data tests check real data.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at metrics, and at how defining a measure once in a semantic layer keeps every report agreeing.

lessons.title: Semantic layers and metrics

lead.text: East has revenue 300 from 5 orders, so its average order value is 60, and West has revenue 900 from 45 orders, so its average is 20.

reveal.text: The overall value is 24. Averaging the two regional figures would give 40, because it treats a region with 5 orders as equal to one with 45.

steps.headline: A metric is a named calculation with an agreed definition, and a semantic layer defines it once for every dashboard.

lead.text: Three dashboards report January revenue and show 900, 800 and 750. None of them is making an arithmetic error. The first counts every order, the second leaves out cancelled orders, and the third also takes off refunds, so each has quietly defined *revenue* for itself. A **metric** is a named calculation with an agreed definition, which fixes the measure being aggregated, the filters applied to it, the grain, and the time dimension it is reported over. Without that, the name stands for several calculations, and nobody can say which number the company should trust.

A **semantic layer** is the place where metrics and dimensions are defined once, so that every dashboard and query asks the layer for revenue instead of writing its own. The layer turns a request, such as revenue by month, into the SQL with the agreed filters. Tools such as dbt's semantic layer keep these definitions in files under version control, where a change is reviewed like code.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the effect. With revenue defined once, as the sum of order amounts excluding cancelled orders, all three dashboards show 800. A change to the definition, such as a new status to exclude, is then made in one place and reaches every report together.

diagram.alt: Two views of January revenue on three dashboards. When each dashboard defines revenue itself the numbers are 900, 800 and 750. When revenue is a metric defined once and reused, all three show 800.

lead.text: The agreed definition of revenue is the sum of order amounts, leaving out cancelled orders. January has orders worth 420 paid, 260 shipped and 90 cancelled.

reveal.text: The filter is part of the metric, so no dashboard has to remember to apply it.

steps.headline: A ratio metric divides one metric by another after both have been aggregated, which is not the same as averaging ratios.

lead.text: Average order value is revenue divided by orders, and it is a **ratio metric**: it is defined from two other metrics, a numerator and a denominator, and the tool divides them *after* aggregating each over whatever groups were asked for. This follows the rule from the lesson on facts, where a ratio is rebuilt from its additive parts and divided last.

The reason shows in the table. East has an average of 60 on 5 orders and West has an average of 20 on 45 orders. Averaging the two averages gives 40, but the business took 1,200 in revenue on 50 orders, which is 24 per order. The average of averages gives each region the same weight, whereas the ratio of totals gives each *order* the same weight, which is what a question about average order value means.
