lead.text: Now take North, with revenue 200 from 10 orders, and South, with revenue 1,000 from 20 orders.

reveal.text: Whatever the regional averages are, the overall figure must come from the totals, and the semantic layer does this automatically for a ratio metric.

steps.headline: Metrics come in four kinds, and what separates them is how the parts are combined.

lead.text: A **simple** metric aggregates one measure, such as revenue as the sum of the order amount. A **ratio** metric divides one metric by another. A **cumulative** metric accumulates a metric over time, such as revenue to date, which adds each month to the running total. A **derived** metric does arithmetic on other metrics, for instance profit as revenue minus cost. These are the kinds that dbt's metric definitions use, and the same split is found in other semantic layers.

The split tells the tool how to build the query. A ratio needs its numerator and denominator aggregated separately before the division, a cumulative metric needs an ordering by time, and a derived metric needs its inputs at the same grain. Most reports need only a handful of simple metrics, and the others follow from them.

A cumulative metric sums a metric over time. A derived metric does arithmetic on metrics, such as profit as revenue minus cost.

Compare with the average of the two regional values.

steps.headline: A distinct count cannot be added across groups, because a customer in two groups is counted in both, so it must be recomputed at the grain requested.

lead.text: Ratios are not the only measures that refuse to add. A count of **distinct customers** is another, and the figure shows why. North has customers 7, 8, 9 and 10, and South has 9, 10 and 11, so the regional counts are 4 and 3. Customers 9 and 10 buy in both regions, so each is counted once in each, and the sum of 7 counts them twice. The number of distinct customers over both regions is 5.

Such measures are **non-additive** in the sense of the second lesson: no sum over groups gives the right answer, and the figure must be recomputed over the union at whatever grain is asked for. This is another reason for a semantic layer. A metric defined as a distinct count tells the tool to count again over the requested group, by region, by month or in total, and nobody has to remember to avoid adding regional figures together.

diagram.alt: Two overlapping circles of customers. North holds customers 7, 8, 9 and 10 and South holds 9, 10 and 11. Customers 9 and 10 are in both. Adding the region counts gives 7, but there are only 5 distinct customers.

lead.text: A ratio can have a non-additive part. North has revenue 700 and 4 distinct customers, and South has revenue 300 and 3 distinct customers, with 2 customers shared between them.

reveal.text: Revenue adds across regions and distinct customers do not, so the numerator and the denominator each have to be rebuilt for the whole group before dividing.

lessons.orientation: Define a metric once, compute ratios from totals, and avoid double counting distinct values.
lessons.nextAction: Trace data upstream and downstream through a lineage graph and count what a change affects.

blocks.text: A finance team and a sales team each report revenue for January and arrive at 800 and 900, both from the same orders. The difference is a single filter: one team leaves out cancelled orders and the other does not. Each number is correct under its own definition, and the company has two, under one name.

This is the problem that a semantic layer addresses. It keeps one definition of each metric, with its measure, filters and grain, and builds the query for each request. This lesson covers what a metric is, how its kinds differ, and why ratios and distinct counts must be rebuilt, not added.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to define a metric once from additive parts, explain why a ratio of totals differs from an average of ratios, and avoid double counting distinct measures.
intro.whyItMatters: Two numbers for one name destroy trust faster than a wrong number does.

recap.keyIdea: A metric is defined once with its measure, filters and grain, and ratios and distinct counts are rebuilt from totals at the requested grain, never added.

blocks.text: A metric names a calculation and fixes its measure, filters and grain, and a semantic layer keeps one definition for every dashboard. Ratio metrics divide totals that have been aggregated first, which is why the overall average order value differs from the average of regional ones.
A distinct count cannot be added across groups either, since a customer in two groups is counted in each, so such measures are recomputed over the group that is asked for.

recap.nextHook: The next module starts with lineage, which traces where a number came from and what depends on it.

lessons.title: Lineage

lead.text: A team writes down its connections as arrows. The source crm feeds stg_crm, which feeds int_customer_orders, which feeds mart_revenue and mart_marketing. The revenue mart feeds dash_sales and dash_exec, and the marketing mart feeds dash_exec as well.

reveal.text: Five nodes, although stg_crm has only one direct consumer. The graph on the next screen shows the whole picture.

steps.headline: Upstream nodes feed a dataset and downstream nodes consume it, directly or through others, so lineage is a graph of what was built from what.

lead.text: **Lineage** is a record of which datasets and jobs produced which other datasets, so that any number can be traced back to its sources and forward to its uses. It is a graph, with an arrow from each dataset to the datasets built from it, and two words describe positions in it. The nodes **upstream** of a dataset are everything it is built from, at any distance back to the sources, and the nodes **downstream** are everything built from it, at any distance forward to the dashboards.

The figure draws eleven nodes. Select downstream of stg_crm and the graph highlights five nodes: the model that reads it, the two marts that read that, and the two dashboards that read the marts, even though stg_crm itself has only one direct consumer. Select upstream of dash_exec and nine nodes light up, which is every model and source it depends on.

afterFigure.text: Both are the same walk run in opposite directions. Going upstream answers where a number came from, and going downstream answers what uses it. The count includes every node on *any* path, so a node reached by two routes, such as the revenue mart, is counted once.

diagram.alt: A lineage graph of eleven nodes. Three sources, crm, shop and ads, feed three staging models. Two staging models feed int_customer_orders, which feeds mart_revenue and mart_marketing, and stg_ads also feeds mart_marketing. The marts feed two dashboards, dash_sales and dash_exec. The views highlight everything downstream of stg_crm and everything upstream of dash_exec.

steps.headline: Walking downstream from a node that is about to change lists the models, reports and owners that the change can break.

lead.text: Suppose the ads source changes the shape of its data. The nodes downstream of it, in the first view of the figure, are stg_ads, mart_marketing and dash_exec, so the change can break one dashboard and no more. Doing this *before* the change is called an **impact analysis**: walk downstream from the node that will change, and every model, report and owner on the way is someone to warn or something to test.

The answer depends on where the change is. A change to crm, in the second view, reaches six nodes and both dashboards, because customer data is used by the revenue and marketing paths alike. Without a graph the question is answered from memory, and the dashboard that nobody remembered is the one that breaks.

afterFigure.text: An impact analysis counts only direct consumers if it is done carelessly. The dashboards are rarely connected to a source by a single arrow, and a change reaches them through every hop, so the whole downstream set is what matters.

steps.headline: Jobs can emit run events that name their inputs and outputs, and a lineage store assembles those events into the graph.

lead.text: A graph drawn by hand is out of date the first time a job changes. A graph assembled from what jobs really did stays true, and that is what an open standard such as **OpenLineage** provides. Each time a job runs it emits a **run event**, which says that a run of a named job has started or completed, and lists the datasets that the job read, its *inputs*, and the datasets that it wrote, its *outputs*. A lineage store collects the events and joins them into a graph, adding an edge from every input to every output of a run.

The figure steps through three events. The first says that build_stg_crm read crm and wrote stg_crm, which adds one edge. The second does the same for shop, and the third says that build_int read both staging models and wrote int_customer_orders, which joins the two chains. No one drew the graph: it appeared as the jobs ran.

steps.headline: Table-level lineage shows which datasets depend on each other, and column-level lineage narrows a change to the columns that use it.

lead.text: A table-level graph has a limit. If the column amt in the shop source is renamed, every dataset downstream of the shop table is flagged, and with it all five columns of mart_revenue, although only two of them are computed from amt. **Column-level lineage** records, for each output column, which input columns it was derived from, and so narrows the warning: only revenue and tax read shop.amt, and order_id, order_date and region are safe.

OpenLineage can carry this detail on an output dataset as an extra, called a facet, and many lineage tools can also work it out by reading the SQL. The table-level graph is still the right first view, and the column-level one is the second, used when the table-level count is too large to act on.

blocks.text: A column in a source system is renamed on a Friday. On Monday a dashboard that nobody connected to that system fails to load, and the person who owns the dashboard has to find out why. They would need to know which models read the column, which read those models, and which of those feed the dashboard, and that knowledge usually exists only in the heads of a few people.

Lineage writes it down. It is the record of which datasets and jobs produced which others, and it answers two questions that come up constantly: where did this number come from, and what will break if this changes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a lineage graph to list what is upstream or downstream of a node, and say what impact analysis and column-level lineage add.
intro.whyItMatters: Lineage turns a guess about what a change will break into a list.

recap.keyIdea: Lineage is a graph of which datasets were built from which, and walking it upstream finds a number's sources and walking it downstream finds what a change will break.

blocks.text: Upstream is everything a dataset is built from and downstream is everything built from it, at any distance. An impact analysis walks downstream from the node that will change and lists every model, report and owner on the way.
Lineage that comes from run events stays true as jobs change, and column-level lineage narrows a table-level warning to the columns that really depend on the changed one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson measures quality: how complete, unique and fresh a dataset is, and how unusual a value is.

lessons.title: Measuring quality

lead.text: A customer table has 2,000 rows, and 1,840 of them have a postcode filled in. A team asks how complete the postcode column is.

reveal.text: The column is 92% complete, which is a rate and not a verdict. Whether 92% is good enough is the next question, and the answer depends on what the data is for.

steps.headline: Data can be wrong in six distinct ways, called quality dimensions, and each one asks a different question of the data.

lead.text: Saying that data is *bad* is no help to the person who has to repair it, because the repair depends on how it is bad. A common list names six **quality dimensions**. **Completeness** asks whether the values are present, and **uniqueness** whether each thing is recorded once. **Validity** asks whether a value follows the rules for its kind, such as a date falling in a sensible range. **Accuracy** asks whether it matches the real world, **consistency** whether two sources agree about it, and **timeliness** whether it is recent enough for its use.

The figure puts a question and an example against each. The dimensions differ in what is needed to check them. Completeness, uniqueness and validity can be checked from the data alone, and a rule or a test will find the fault. Consistency needs a second source to compare with, and accuracy needs a reference from outside, such as a postal address file, so a rule alone cannot establish it.

afterFigure.text: A date of birth in the year 2090 is therefore a validity failure, since a rule can catch it. A date of birth that is a plausible but wrong date is an accuracy failure, which only an outside record can reveal.

diagram.alt: A table of six data quality dimensions with a question and an example for each: completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency and timeliness.
diagram.caption: Each dimension asks a different question of the data.

lead.text: Consider a table of people in which one row has a birth date in the year 2090, and every other value looks ordinary.

reveal.text: A rule that no one is born in the future would catch it, which tells you the dimension needs no outside reference.

steps.headline: Each dimension becomes a rate, which is compared with a target agreed with the people who use the data.

lead.text: Each dimension can be turned into a number: **completeness** is the non-null rows over all rows, so 1,840 of 2,000 is 92%, and **uniqueness** is the distinct values over all rows, so 450 distinct order ids in 500 rows is 90%. Validity is the rows that pass the rule over all rows, and the others follow the same pattern. A rate, unlike a pass or fail, says *how far* the data is from perfect, and can be tracked over time.

A rate means something only against a target, and the target comes from the use. The same table, with the three rates in the figure, is good enough for a marketing list, where a missing email costs one mailing, and not good enough for a billing run, where a repeated order id could mean charging twice. The targets are therefore agreed with the users of the data, and written down next to the rates they apply to.

reveal.text: A uniqueness below 100% means that some ids repeat, and the duplicate test from the lesson on testing finds which ones.

steps.headline: A z-score measures how many standard deviations today's count lies from the recent mean, and flags a day whose volume is unusual.

lead.text: A table can be complete, unique and valid and still be wrong because half of it is missing, and the rates above would not notice, since they judge the rows that exist. A volume check judges *how many* rows arrived. A fixed limit, say at least 1,000 rows a day, soon goes wrong: volumes grow and have weekly patterns, so a limit that is right in January is too low by June. The check instead compares today with recent history.

The comparison is a **z-score**, the distance of today's count from the recent mean, measured in standard deviations. The history in the figure is 200, 220, 200 and 220 thousand rows, which has a mean of 210 and a population standard deviation of 10, found by dividing by the number of days. A count of 215 has a z-score of 0.5 and is ordinary. A count of 175 has (175 − 210) / 10 = −3.5, well below the lower dashed line at three standard deviations, and the usual practice is to raise an alert when the score passes 3 in either direction.

afterFigure.text: The three-deviation line is a convention and not a law. Teams widen or narrow it according to how costly a false alarm is compared with a missed fault.

In the first view today is 215, inside the lines, with a z-score of 0.5. In the second today is 175, below the lower line, with a z-score of minus 3.5.

reveal.text: A score this far below the mean is a strong sign that something upstream did not deliver, and a person should look before the report goes out.

steps.headline: Find the z-score of today's count of 100 against the recent counts 80, 90, 80 and 90.

workedSteps.text: Find the mean of the four recent counts.
Find how far each count lies from the mean, and square it, so that distances in both directions count as positive.
The population variance is the mean of the squares, and the standard deviation is its square root.
Today is 15 above the mean, and 15 divided by 5 is the z-score.

steps.headline: Find the z-score of today's count of 380 against the recent counts 300, 340, 300 and 340.

workedSteps.text: The mean is 320 and each count lies 20 from it, so the squares are all 400 and the standard deviation is 20.
Today is above the mean, so the score will be positive.
Divide by the standard deviation to get the z-score.

steps.headline: Timeliness is measured as the age of the data against a target, and a breach is the amount by which the age exceeds the target.

lead.text: The last dimension is the simplest to measure. The **age** of a table is the time since it was last updated, and its **freshness target** is the age the users can tolerate. A table last updated at 05:30, with a target of three hours, is allowed to reach 08:30. Checked at 07:30 its age is two hours, inside the target. Checked at 11:00 its age is 5.5 hours, and the **breach** is the part beyond the target, 5.5 − 3 = 2.5 hours.

Expressing the result as the excess, and not just as pass or fail, matters because breaches differ in size: a table 10 minutes late and one a day late both fail, but they call for different responses. Freshness targets are also the commonest kind of service level between the team that builds a table and the people who use it, which the next lesson takes up.

diagram.alt: A clock axis from 05:00 to 12:00 with a table updated at 05:30 and a 3-hour allowance ending at 08:30. Checked at 07:30 the table is 2 hours old, inside the target. Checked at 11:00 it is 5.5 hours old, which is 2.5 hours over the target.

reveal.text: The age is worked out first and the target is taken off it, and a negative result would mean that the table is within its target.

lead.text: Weekday counts average 210 thousand, but Saturdays are quiet. The last four Saturdays had counts of 80, 100, 80 and 100, so their mean is 90 and their population standard deviation is 10. This Saturday has 120.

reveal.text: Comparing with the weekday mean would have raised a false alarm in the other direction. The baseline has to match the pattern the data follows.

lessons.orientation: Compute quality rates, a z-score for volume and a freshness breach.
lessons.nextAction: Classify changes against a data contract, compute an error budget, and assign ownership.

blocks.text: A table of 1,250 customers, 1,000 of which have an email address, is 80% complete. The figure is more useful than a statement that the data is mostly fine, because it can be compared with a target, tracked from one week to the next and attached to a particular column.

Quality can be measured in this way along several lines at once. This lesson names the dimensions along which data can be wrong, turns three of them into rates, and adds two checks that catch faults no row-level rule can: a z-score for an unusual volume, and a freshness target for a table that stopped updating.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute completeness, uniqueness and freshness, and use a z-score against recent history to flag an abnormal volume.
intro.whyItMatters: A number can be tracked and argued about, while a feeling that the data is bad cannot.

recap.keyIdea: Quality is measured as a rate for each dimension and judged against a target that matches the use, with a z-score for volume and an age for freshness.

blocks.text: Data can be wrong in six ways, completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, and each of the first three can be turned into a rate such as non-null rows over all rows. A rate is judged against a target agreed with the users, so the same table can be good enough for one use and not for another.
A z-score compares today's row count with recent history, in standard deviations, and a freshness check measures the age of the table against its target and reports the breach as the excess.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns targets like these into agreements: contracts, ownership and service levels with an error budget.

lessons.title: Contracts, ownership and service levels

lead.text: A table of orders is read by four reports. Three of them select the column order_total by name, and the fourth reads only order_id. The team that produces the table renames order_total to total.

reveal.text: Three reports fail on the next run, and the producer may not have known that any of them existed. A contract is how the producer finds out first.

steps.headline: A data contract is an agreement between a producer and its consumers on a dataset's schema, meaning, quality and timeliness, and it is checked automatically.

lead.text: A **data contract** is an agreement between the team that produces a dataset and the teams that use it. It says what the dataset contains, which is its *schema*, what the columns mean, how good the values must be, and how fresh the data must be. The figure shows one as a file kept beside the code: the dataset has a named owner, a schema with required and optional columns, a quality section with rules such as order_id never being null, and a service-level section that says when the data is ready.

What makes it a contract and not documentation is that a machine checks it. In dbt a model contract makes the build fail if the model's output does not have the columns and types it promised, and the Open Data Contract Standard describes the schema, quality and service-level parts in one YAML document that tools can read. A written agreement that nothing checks drifts away from the data within months, and then nobody trusts it.

diagram.alt: A contract file for a dataset called orders_daily with an owner and three sections. The schema lists order_id, order_total and an optional delivered_at. The quality section says order_id is never null and order_total is at least 99 percent complete. The service level says the data is ready by 07:00 on 90 percent of days over 30 days.

steps.headline: A change that alters a field a consumer relies on is breaking, and a change that only adds something optional is compatible.

lead.text: The contract exists to make changes safe, and the first thing it needs is a way to sort them. A **breaking change** is one after which an existing consumer fails or gets something different: removing a field, renaming it, changing its type, and changing its *meaning*, as when a price that included tax now excludes it. The last is the most dangerous, since the column keeps its name and type and every query still runs. A **compatible change** leaves everything a consumer relied on as it was, as when an optional column or a new table is added.

The sorting is a rule of thumb, and consumers have the last word. A new column is compatible for a consumer that names the columns it wants, but it can break one that selects every column into a fixed schema. That is why the contract also records who consumes the dataset, so that a producer can see who to ask before a change.

reveal.text: A change that is breaking is announced, versioned and given a date, and a compatible one can simply be released.

steps.headline: A service-level objective sets a target for a measurable indicator, and the error budget is the failure it allows.

lead.text: A contract also promises timeliness, and a promise needs a number. The thing measured is the **service-level indicator**, such as whether the table was ready by 07:00 on a given day. The **service-level objective** is the target for it over a period: ready on 90% of days over a 30-day month. Nothing in practice is perfect, so the objective is less than 100%, and the gap, one minus the objective, is the **error budget**. Ninety per cent of 30 days is 27 days, which leaves a budget of 3 failed days.

The same arithmetic works in hours. An objective of 99% of the time over 720 hours allows 1% failure, or 7.2 hours, and 99.9% allows 0.72 hours, which is 43.2 minutes. In the figure each failed day spends one of the three blocks. With two failures one block is left, with three the budget is spent, and a fourth failure takes the month to 26 of 30 days, below the 90%.

afterFigure.text: The budget is useful because it can be spent. A team with budget left may ship a risky change, and a team that has spent it should spend its time on reliability instead. A stricter objective costs more to meet, so it is set to match what the consumers really need.

steps.headline: The producing team owns a dataset's meaning and its failures, the platform team owns the tooling, and consumers are told.

lead.text: A contract and an objective are useless if nobody is accountable for them. The usual arrangement gives each role a clear part. The **producer**, the team in whose domain the data originates, owns the dataset, its meaning and its quality, because only that team knows what a field really is and why it changed. The **platform** team owns the scheduler, the storage and the checks that run, but does not decide what a field means. **Consumers** own their own reports, and rely on being told.

The roles show most clearly when a freshness check fails at 07:00. The producer is paged, since it can fix the pipeline, and tells the consumers; the platform keeps the alerts working; the consumers hold back reports that depend on the late table. Giving everything to the pipeline team is the mistake to avoid, because it can repair a pipeline but cannot say what a changed field was supposed to mean.

diagram.alt: A table of three roles. The producer owns the dataset and its meaning, and is paged and tells consumers when a freshness check fails. The platform team owns the scheduler and tooling and keeps checks and alerts running. The consumer owns its reports, is told, and holds back its own reports.

blocks.text: The producer of an orders table decides one afternoon to rename order_total to total, which is tidier. Nothing in the producer's own tests fails. The next morning three reports are empty, and the people who built them learn why from the person who sits next to them, who learned from someone else.

A data contract is a way to make that conversation happen before the change, and to make it a matter of agreed terms and not of luck. This lesson covers what a contract says, which changes break it, how a promise about timeliness becomes an objective with an error budget, and who is accountable when something fails.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a schema change as breaking or compatible, work out an error budget from an objective, and say who owns a failing dataset.
intro.whyItMatters: A change that nobody was told about costs more than the change itself.

recap.keyIdea: A data contract is a machine-checked agreement on schema, meaning, quality and timeliness, and its objective leaves an error budget that the producer is accountable for.

blocks.text: A contract sorts changes into breaking ones, which remove, rename or retype a field or change its meaning, and compatible ones, which only add something optional. A timeliness promise becomes a service-level objective, and one minus the objective, taken over the period, is the error budget: 1% of 720 hours is 7.2 hours.
The producing team owns the meaning and the failures of its dataset, the platform team owns the tooling, and consumers are told when something breaks.

lessons.title: Classifying and protecting data

lead.text: A table stores the sha-256 hash of each customer's email, instead of the email. Someone holds a list of 50,000 candidate emails, and wants to know which one belongs to a particular hash.

reveal.text: At most 50,000 hashes, which a laptop does in a moment. The hash was meant to hide the email, and a guessable email makes it little protection.

steps.headline: Data is labelled by sensitivity, and personal data includes indirect identifiers, so a column that looks harmless can still need protection.

lead.text: Protection starts with knowing what you hold. **Classification** gives each dataset or column a label for its sensitivity, commonly public, internal, confidential or restricted, and the label drives who may see it and how it is stored. In the figure product names are public, order totals internal, and an email, a postcode and a date of birth are confidential, while free-text health notes are restricted, since GDPR treats health data as special category data.

Which columns are *personal data* is not limited to names. Under GDPR it is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, so a column counts if it can identify someone *indirectly*, alone or combined with others. A postcode, an age band and a sex together can single a person out, even though none of them is a name. Latanya Sweeney found in 1990 US census data that about 87% of people were unique on five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth, and the finding shaped the field.

diagram.alt: A table of six customer columns with a sensitivity label each: product_name is public, order_total is internal, email, postcode and date_of_birth are confidential, and health_note is restricted.
diagram.caption: The label decides who may see a column and how it is stored.

steps.headline: Replacing identifiers with tokens or hashes is pseudonymisation, which leaves personal data, whereas true anonymisation cannot be linked back.

lead.text: **Pseudonymisation** replaces an identifier with something else, such as a random token or a hash, so that the data can no longer be attributed to a person without additional information. GDPR still counts such data as personal, because the additional information exists somewhere. **Anonymisation** goes further: the data cannot be linked back to a person by any reasonably likely means, and only then does it fall outside data protection law. Where the exact legal line falls depends on the jurisdiction, so this lesson gives the technical picture and not legal advice.

A hash is often mistaken for anonymisation. An unsalted hash of an email is the same for everyone, so anybody can hash a list of guessed emails and compare, and the hidden value is recovered. Adding a random **salt** to each record before hashing defeats precomputed tables, because every record needs its own guesses, but it is still pseudonymisation: whoever holds the salt can re-link the record.

diagram.alt: Two ways to hash an email. In the first an unsalted hash is the same for everyone, so a list of guessed emails can be hashed and compared. In the second a separate random salt is added to each record before hashing, so precomputed tables do not work, but the result is still pseudonymous.
diagram.caption: Hashing hides an email only from someone who cannot guess it. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Each of 1,000 records is now hashed with its own random salt, and the attacker still holds 50,000 candidate emails.

reveal.text: A salt raises the cost of an attack but does not change what kind of data it is.

steps.headline: A table is k-anonymous when every combination of quasi-identifiers appears at least k times, so no row is alone in its group.

lead.text: Removing the names does not make a table anonymous, because the remaining columns can identify people in combination. The columns that do so, such as age band, postcode prefix and sex, are called **quasi-identifiers**. A table has **k-anonymity**, a model introduced by Sweeney in 2002, when every combination of quasi-identifier values is shared by at least k rows, so that anyone who knows a person's values finds at least k candidate rows and cannot say which is theirs. The value of **k** for a table is the size of its *smallest* group.

The figure shows nine rows. As collected they form groups of 4, 3, 1 and 1 rows, so k is 1: two people are unique and anyone who knows their age band, postcode and sex finds them. Generalising the values, by dropping the sex column and then widening the age band to 20-39, merges the small groups, and the groups become 6 and 3, which is k = 3.

afterFigure.text: Generalising loses detail, and removing the offending rows, called suppression, loses people. The choice between them depends on what the analysis needs.

diagram.alt: A table of nine people with age band, postcode prefix and sex, and the size of each group of identical rows. As collected the groups have 4, 3, 1 and 1 rows, so k is 1. With sex removed the groups are 5, 3 and 1, still k of 1. With age widened to 20 to 39 as well, the groups are 6 and 3, so k is 3.
diagram.caption: Generalising the columns merges small groups. Use the buttons to follow the steps.

lead.text: The nine rows of the figure form groups of 4, 3, 1 and 1 on age band, postcode prefix and sex.

reveal.text: Counting the rows in small groups tells you how much has to be generalised or removed to reach the k you want.

steps.headline: Find k for six rows with (age band, postcode): (20-29, N1) twice, (30-39, N1) once and (30-39, N2) three times.

workedSteps.text: Group identical rows and count each group.
k is the size of the smallest group, since the weakest group is the most exposed.
So the table is 1-anonymous, however large the other groups are.

steps.headline: Widen the age band to 20-39 and find k again.

workedSteps.text: The rows (20-29, N1) and (30-39, N1) now share a band and a postcode.
The rows (30-39, N2) become (20-39, N2).
Find k from the two group sizes.

steps.headline: k-anonymity is a floor, not a guarantee, because groups can still reveal a sensitive value and other columns can still single a person out.

lead.text: A table with k = 3 means that no person is alone in their group on the *chosen* quasi-identifiers, and that is all. If all three people in a group have the same diagnosis, knowing someone is in the group reveals it. Other columns that were not chosen as quasi-identifiers, or data held elsewhere, may still single a person out, which is why combinations of ordinary columns, and not only columns marked as personal, have to be checked.

The same point applies to every technique in this lesson. A label, a hash and a k each reduce risk and none removes it, so the practical question is how much risk the purpose allows. The next lesson looks at the law that sets those limits.
The nine-row table has groups of 4, 3, 1 and 1 rows. Instead of generalising, the rows in groups smaller than 3 are removed to reach k = 3.

reveal.text: Removing rows keeps the remaining values exact but loses the people removed, so generalising is the choice when every person matters to the analysis.

lessons.orientation: Classify columns, tell pseudonymisation from anonymisation, and compute k.
lessons.nextAction: Apply GDPR principles, lawful bases and rights, and plan an erasure in a data lake.

blocks.text: Latanya Sweeney analysed 1990 US census data and found that about 87% of people could be picked out by just three values: five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth. None of the three is a name, and none would normally be marked as personal, yet together they identify most people.

This is why removing names from a table does not make it anonymous, and why protecting data begins with asking what a combination of columns reveals. This lesson sorts data by sensitivity, separates pseudonymisation from anonymisation, and measures the risk of re-identification with k.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify data by sensitivity, tell hashing and pseudonymisation from anonymisation, and compute k for a table.
intro.whyItMatters: Data that looks harmless can identify people once its columns are combined.

recap.keyIdea: Personal data includes combinations of ordinary columns, pseudonymised data is still personal, and k, the smallest group size on the quasi-identifiers, measures how easily rows are re-identified.

blocks.text: Data is labelled by sensitivity, and personal data includes indirect identifiers such as a postcode and an age together. Hashing or tokenising an identifier is pseudonymisation, which leaves personal data, because a guessable value can be matched and the extra information can re-link it.
A table is k-anonymous when every combination of quasi-identifiers is shared by at least k rows, k is the smallest group size, and generalising or suppressing rows raises it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the law, and to what the GDPR requires when you hold personal data.

lessons.title: Privacy law in practice

lead.text: A customer asks to be erased, and the engineer runs a DELETE on a versioned lakehouse table. The data was held in the current table, in the old data files on storage, and in the backups.

reveal.text: Two of the three still hold it. The DELETE changed only what the table returns today.

steps.headline: Seven principles govern how personal data may be handled, and each one turns into a design decision for engineers.

lead.text: The GDPR, the EU regulation that has applied since May 2018, starts from principles in Article 5. Data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; collected for specified purposes and not used for others, which is *purpose limitation*; limited to what is needed, which is *data minimisation*; kept accurate; kept no longer than necessary, which is *storage limitation*; and kept secure, which the regulation calls integrity and confidentiality. The seventh, *accountability*, makes the **controller**, the organisation that decides why and how the data is used, responsible for showing that it complies.

These are often treated as a matter for the legal team, but most of them are built by engineers. Minimisation is a decision about which columns to load, storage limitation is a retention setting and a job that deletes on time, and accountability is the records and logs that can be shown to a regulator. This course used [[personal data|Information relating to an identifiable person, including indirect identifiers. Met in "Classifying and protecting data".]] as the starting point, and these principles say what may then be done with it.

diagram.alt: A table of seven GDPR principles and what each means in practice: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability.
diagram.caption: Each principle turns into a design decision.

reveal.text: A principle that sounds legal usually reduces to a column, a setting or a job.

steps.headline: Processing needs one of six lawful bases, and consent is only one of them.

lead.text: Before personal data is processed, there must be a **lawful basis** for it, and Article 6 lists six: *consent*, *contract*, *legal obligation*, *vital interests*, *public task* and *legitimate interests*. The figure gives an activity for each. Shipping a parcel the customer ordered is needed to perform the contract. Keeping invoices because tax law requires it is a legal obligation. Fraud checks on card payments can rest on the organisation's legitimate interests, and a marketing email usually needs consent.

The common mistake is to treat consent as the only basis. Consent can be withdrawn at any time, so it is a poor basis for anything that must continue, such as the invoice record, and it must be freely given and specific. The right question is which basis genuinely fits the purpose, and the answer is recorded, since accountability requires it. A person's rights also depend on the basis chosen.

reveal.text: The basis is chosen to fit the purpose, and a different basis for the same data may bring different rights for the person.

steps.headline: People have rights over their data, and each right is a task that engineers have to be able to run.

lead.text: A person whose data you hold, called the **data subject**, has rights listed in Articles 15 to 22. They can ask what you hold, which is *access*, have wrong data corrected, which is *rectification*, and in some cases have it deleted, which is *erasure*. They can ask that data be kept but not used, which is *restriction*, receive it in a common format to take elsewhere, which is *portability*, and object to some processing. The controller has to answer without undue delay and in any case within one month.

Each right becomes a task in the figure. Access is an export across every system that holds the person. Rectification must reach every copy, and erasure has to reach files and backups as well as tables. A team that cannot find all of a person's data in a month has a data design problem, not only a legal one, and lineage and classification, from earlier lessons, are what make the search possible.

lead.text: A customer wants all of their order history in a file that they can load into another shop's system.

reveal.text: The right is satisfied by an export job, and the format matters because it has to be reusable.

steps.headline: Deleting a row in a versioned table writes a new version, and the old files hold the data until they are vacuumed and the backups expire.

lead.text: Tables built on immutable files, such as Delta, never change a file in place. A DELETE writes a new version in the log that no longer includes the rows, and the old files remain on storage so that earlier versions can be read, which is what time travel means. The person's data therefore still exists after the DELETE. A **vacuum** removes files that no current version needs and that are older than the *retention period*, which defaults to seven days in Delta, and only then is the data gone from the table's storage.

Backups are a separate copy. A complete erasure plan therefore has three stages, shown in the figure: the DELETE, the vacuum after retention, and the expiry of the last backup that holds the data. Until each stage is done the data exists somewhere, and the plan says how long that takes, so that the answer to the person is accurate.

diagram.alt: Four moments in an erasure. On day 0 the current table, the old files in storage and the backups all hold the data. On day 1 the DELETE is committed and the table no longer holds it, but the old files and backups do. On day 8 a vacuum removes the old files. On day 30 the backups expire and no copy is left.

steps.headline: Plan one erasure: DELETE on day 1, 7 days of retention, and a day-0 backup kept for 30 days.

workedSteps.text: The DELETE writes a new version on day 1. The table stops returning the rows, but the files remain.
The old files can be vacuumed once the retention has passed, 7 days after the commit.
The backup taken on day 0 is kept for 30 days, so it expires on day 30.
The last copy goes with the backup, and that is the date to give the customer.

steps.headline: Plan another erasure: the DELETE is committed on day 2 and the table keeps old files for 14 days.

workedSteps.text: The DELETE removes the rows from the current version on day 2.
The old files are kept for the retention period after the commit.
Work out the earliest day a vacuum can remove them.

steps.headline: A breach must be reported within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, where feasible, and fines are set as a share of turnover.

lead.text: A **personal data breach** is a security incident that leads to the loss, alteration, disclosure of or access to personal data. Under Article 33 the controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. The clock starts at *awareness*, not at the time of the incident, so detection matters: a team that cannot tell when data has leaked cannot meet the deadline.

Fines are set high enough to matter. The most serious infringements, such as breaking the basic principles or the rights of data subjects, can draw a fine of up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, under Article 83(5), and some other infringements, including failing to notify a breach, fall under a lower ceiling. This is educational content and not legal advice, and the law of your own jurisdiction and your own legal team decide what applies.
A controller becomes aware of a breach at 14:00 on Monday, and wants to notify the authority within the 72-hour limit.

reveal.text: A team that logs access and watches for unusual reads starts the clock sooner, and the clock is the thing that cannot be paused.

lead.text: A company has a worldwide annual turnover of 2.5 billion euros. The higher ceiling is 20 million euros or 4% of turnover, whichever is higher.

reveal.text: The percentage limb dominates for any company with a turnover above 500 million euros, which is where 4% reaches 20 million.

lessons.orientation: Explain principles, lawful bases and rights, and plan an erasure in a versioned table.
lessons.nextAction: Assign governance roles, sort metadata, and turn a policy into a control.

blocks.text: A customer writes to ask for their data to be deleted. The engineer runs a DELETE on the customer table and closes the ticket, and then learns that the lakehouse keeps every earlier version of the table for seven days, and that the nightly backups keep the data for thirty.

Privacy law reaches into storage in this way, which is why this lesson treats the GDPR as a set of designs and not as a legal matter. It covers the principles, the six lawful bases, the rights people have over their data, how to plan an erasure in a table of immutable files, and the clock that starts when a breach is noticed. This is educational content, not legal advice.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to explain the main GDPR principles, lawful bases and rights, and plan an erasure in a table format with immutable files.
intro.whyItMatters: Each principle and right becomes something a person has to build.

recap.keyIdea: The GDPR's principles, six lawful bases and rights become engineering tasks, and an erasure in a versioned table is complete only after the vacuum and the backup expiry.

blocks.text: Seven principles set what may be done with personal data, six lawful bases say when processing is allowed, with consent as only one, and rights such as access, erasure and portability each become a task to be run within a month. A breach has to be notified within 72 hours of awareness, where feasible.
A DELETE in a versioned table writes a new version, so the data survives in old files until a vacuum removes them after the retention period, and in backups until they expire.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson puts these pieces together as governance: the roles, the catalogue, and how a policy becomes a control.

lessons.title: Governance in practice

lead.text: A policy says that customer data must be deleted when it is older than 36 months. A table holds one monthly partition for each of the last 40 months.

reveal.text: Four partitions are older than the limit. Someone has to delete them, every month, and show that they did.

steps.headline: The owner is accountable for a dataset, the steward maintains its definitions and quality, and the custodian runs the platform that holds it.

lead.text: **Data governance** is the set of roles, rules and checks that keep data trustworthy and used properly, and it is sometimes imagined as a committee that meets and approves things. In practice it is a small number of named people and some automation. Three roles cover most of it. The **owner** is accountable for a dataset: its use, and its targets for quality and freshness, and is usually a senior person in the business area that produces the data. The **steward** maintains the dataset's definitions and day-to-day quality, often an analyst who knows what the numbers mean. The **custodian** runs the platform that stores and protects it, which is an engineering job.

The roles line up with the earlier lessons. The owner is the producer of a data contract and answers when a service-level objective is missed. The steward writes the glossary term for a metric such as headcount and decides what counts. The custodian runs the checks and the storage. Giving all three to the pipeline team is the usual failure, since that team can repair a pipeline but cannot say what headcount should mean.

diagram.alt: A table of three governance roles. The owner is accountable for use and quality targets, for example the HR director. The steward maintains definitions and day-to-day quality, for example an HR analyst. The custodian runs the platform that stores and protects the data, for example a platform engineer.

lead.text: An analyst in HR writes the definition of "headcount" and checks each month that its numbers look right. The HR director is accountable for the dataset.

reveal.text: The role is defined by the work: maintaining definitions and quality, and not by seniority or by who owns the servers.

steps.headline: A catalogue records technical, business and operational metadata about datasets, and a glossary fixes the meaning of business terms.

lead.text: People cannot trust what they cannot find, and a **data catalogue** is where datasets are found. Each entry records **metadata**, data about the dataset, of three kinds. *Technical* metadata describes structure: the schema and the data types. *Business* metadata says what it means and who answers for it: the description, the owner, the classification and the glossary term. *Operational* metadata describes behaviour: when it was last refreshed, how many rows it has and how often it is queried. A **glossary** fixes the meaning of business terms such as headcount, so that the word means one thing across reports.

A catalogue does not fill itself. A scan can collect the technical and operational fields, and lineage from run events, which the lineage lesson described, can fill itself. A description, an owner, a classification and a glossary term need a person, which is why the steward matters. A catalogue full of blank descriptions is a list of table names.

diagram.alt: A catalogue entry for a dataset called hr_headcount_monthly with nine fields. Schema and data types are technical metadata. Description, owner, glossary term and classification are business metadata. Last refresh, row count and query frequency are operational metadata. A second view shows that scans fill the technical and operational fields and a person fills the business ones.

steps.headline: A policy becomes a rule that the platform enforces, with monitoring and evidence, and not a document to remember.

lead.text: A policy states an intention, such as keeping customer data for no more than 36 months, and a policy that lives only in a document depends on every person remembering it. It becomes real by climbing a ladder. The policy is turned into a precise **rule**, rows older than 36 months must not exist. The rule is enforced by a **control**, a scheduled job that deletes those rows. A **monitor**, a check that counts rows older than 36 months and alerts if it finds any, shows whether the control works. The last rung is the **evidence**: the job log and the check results, kept so that an auditor can be shown the policy in operation.

The same ladder applies to the other policies in this course. A rule that salary is visible only to HR becomes a masking rule on the classified column, enforced by the platform for every other role. The principle is that each rung is something a machine does or records, and the person who wrote the policy can rely on it without checking by hand. A policy with nothing beneath it is a hope.

diagram.alt: A ladder of five rungs, policy, rule, control, monitoring and evidence, with an example for a 36-month retention policy at each rung: the policy text, the rule, a scheduled delete job, a check that counts old rows, and the job log and check results kept as evidence.
diagram.caption: A policy becomes enforceable one rung at a time. Use the buttons to climb the ladder for a retention policy.

steps.headline: Turn the policy "salary is visible only to HR" into a control.

workedSteps.text: Classify the column. A salary is personal and confidential, so it is labelled confidential in the catalogue.
State the rule exactly: the column is returned in full to the HR role and masked for every other role.
The control is a masking policy on the column that the platform applies to every query.
Monitor it with a log of who reads the column, and keep the log as evidence.

steps.headline: Turn an 18-month retention policy into a job, and size the first run on a table with one row for each of the last 26 months.

workedSteps.text: The rule is that rows older than 18 months must not exist.
The job deletes every row older than that, and the check counts what is left over, which must be zero.
Work out how many rows the first run deletes.

steps.headline: A certified dataset has been reviewed, owned and monitored, so a badge tells consumers which source to trust.

lead.text: A catalogue can hold hundreds of datasets, and two of them may look alike, as in the figure: a monthly headcount table and a temporary copy of it. A **certified dataset** carries a badge showing that it passes a short checklist, and the checklist draws on the whole course: an owner is named, its terms are defined in the glossary, its tests pass, it is fresh within its objective, its columns are classified, and its lineage is visible. The badge is a quick answer for a consumer who has to choose.

This is what governance that people follow looks like. It is not a committee that must approve each query, but a set of roles, a catalogue, controls the platform enforces, and a visible mark of which data meets the standard. People choose the certified dataset because it is easier and safer to use, and the work of governing is spent where it earns that trust.

diagram.alt: Two datasets side by side. hr_headcount_monthly is certified and meets all six conditions: owner named, definition in the glossary, tests passing, fresh within its objective, classification set and lineage visible. hr_headcount_tmp has no badge and meets only two: tests passing and lineage visible.
diagram.caption: The badge tells a consumer which dataset has been reviewed, owned and monitored.

reveal.text: The missing conditions are a to-do list for the owner and steward, and a badge follows when the list is empty.

lead.text: A catalogue lists 40 datasets and 25 have a named owner. A governance target says every dataset needs one.

reveal.text: Coverage counts such as this are what a governance process tracks, since they show where the work remains.

lessons.orientation: Assign governance roles, sort metadata, and turn a policy into a control.
lessons.nextAction: You can now declare a grain and model history, build and test layered models, define metrics once, trace lineage, measure quality, read a contract, classify and protect personal data, and say who owns what.

blocks.text: A company has a rule that customer data is deleted after 36 months. The rule is in a policy document that was approved by a committee, and nobody can say whether it is followed, because nobody is responsible for the table, nothing runs the deletion, and no check would notice if it stopped.

Governance is what closes that gap. It names the people who are accountable, records what datasets exist and what they mean, and turns each policy into something the platform enforces and can prove. This lesson puts the roles, the catalogue and the controls together, and shows what a trusted dataset looks like at the end.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to assign owner, steward and custodian roles, sort metadata into its three kinds, and turn a policy into a control with a check and evidence.
intro.whyItMatters: A rule that nothing enforces and nobody checks is a hope.

recap.keyIdea: Governance is named owners, stewards and custodians, a catalogue with meaning written in it, and policies turned into enforced and monitored controls.

blocks.text: The owner is accountable for a dataset, the steward maintains its definitions and quality, and the custodian runs the platform. A catalogue holds technical, business and operational metadata, of which only the business kind needs a person to write it.
A policy climbs from rule to control to monitoring to evidence, and a certified dataset is the visible result: owned, defined, tested, fresh, classified and traceable.

questions.prompt: A table has one row per order line. Order 1001 has two lines, of 20.00 and 30.00, and carries a shipping fee of 5.00. The fee is copied onto both rows. What does the fee column add up to?
hints: Count how many rows carry the fee.
SUM adds the value on every row.
Multiply the fee by the number of rows that hold it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fee appears on two rows, so SUM adds 5.00 twice: 5.00 + 5.00 = 10.00.

questions.onCorrect: The fee was charged once, but the column repeats it on each line, so a sum over lines returns 10.00 instead of 5.00.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fee charged once. The column holds it on each of the two rows, and SUM adds every row.
That adds the line amounts, 20.00 + 30.00 + 5.00, which mixes two different columns.

questions.prompt: The grain is one row per order line. Which of these columns is not true at that grain?
hints: Ask of each column whether it describes one line or the whole order.

acceptedIdeas: Shipping fee for the whole order
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shipping fee for the whole order

questions.onCorrect: The fee describes the order, so it belongs in a table with order grain.

misconceptions.feedback: Each line has its own quantity, so it is true at the line grain.
Each line has its own unit price, so it is true at the line grain.
Each line has its own amount, quantity times unit price, so it is true at the line grain.

choices.label: Quantity ordered
Unit price
Shipping fee for the whole order
Line amount

questions.prompt: Why is each order total added once for every line the order has?
hints: Think about how many rows an order with three lines occupies.

acceptedIdeas: SUM adds every row, and each row repeats its order's total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SUM adds every row, and each row repeats its order's total

questions.onCorrect: An order with three lines contributes three rows, each carrying its total, so the total is counted three times.

misconceptions.feedback: SUM does not look at the orders. It adds each row it is given once.
The data type plays no part. The same number simply sits on several rows.
No join is involved here. The repetition is in the table itself.

choices.label: SUM adds every row, and each row repeats its order's total
SUM adds every order twice by default
The order total is a different data type
The orders were joined to the wrong table

questions.prompt: Orders of 50, 70 and 90 have 2, 4 and 1 lines, and each line row repeats its order total. What does SUM(order_total) over the line table return?
hints: Multiply each order total by its number of lines.
Do that for all three orders.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: The line table counts each order once per line, so the sum is 470 although the orders came to 210.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the three orders, 50 + 70 + 90. The line table repeats each total once per line.
That counts the lines. The column holds the order totals, which are added up.

questions.prompt: The retail sales fact table has four dimensions: date, store, product and customer. Each fact row points at exactly one row in each. How many foreign key columns does it hold at least?
hints: Each row points at one row of each dimension.
Count the dimensions.
One key column links to one dimension.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One foreign key per dimension, so 4.

questions.onCorrect: Each foreign key names a row in one dimension, so a star with four dimensions needs at least four.

misconceptions.feedback: One key would point at only one dimension. Each dimension needs its own.
That adds the fact table itself. The keys point at dimensions only.

questions.prompt: Each order carries a shipping fee of 5.00, copied onto every line row. Order 1 has 4 lines and order 2 has 1 line. By how much does SUM(fee) over the line table exceed the fees actually charged?
hints: Work out the sum over lines first.
Then work out what was really charged, once per order.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The table sums 5.00 × 4 + 5.00 × 1 = 25.00, while 2 fees were charged: 10.00. The excess is 15.00.

questions.onCorrect: Moving the fee to an order table would sum to 10.00 exactly, since each order then has one row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum over the line table. The question asks how far it is above the fees charged.
That is the fees actually charged, 2 × 5.00, not the excess.

questions.prompt: Which is a well-formed grain statement for a sales fact table?
hints: A grain statement says what one row stands for.
Look for the one that you could use to count the rows.

acceptedIdeas: One row per product on each receipt line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One row per product on each receipt line

questions.onCorrect: Only the third says what one row is, which tells you what a count of rows would mean.

misconceptions.feedback: A word like this names a topic but does not say what one row is.
This names a period, but a row could be a store, a product or a till.
Everything about customers is a subject, not the definition of a row.

choices.label: Sales
Daily sales data
One row per product on each receipt line
Everything about customers

questions.prompt: Orders of 100, 200 and 300 have 2, 1 and 3 order lines. An order_total column is copied onto each line. What does SUM(order_total) over the line table return?
hints: Each total appears once for every line.
Multiply each order total by its line count.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: The sum counts each order once per line, so it overstates the 600 of the orders by 700.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the three orders. The line table repeats each total once per line.
That counts the lines. The column being summed holds the totals.

questions.prompt: "How long does it take to ship an order after payment?" Which business process does the model record? Answer in two words.
hints: Which activity packs and ships what was ordered?
The process is named for the activity, not for the table.
questions.onCorrect: Fulfilment leaves a payment time and a shipped time, so it can answer how long shipping takes.

misconceptions.feedback: Order taking records what was bought and at what price. It does not record when the parcel left.

questions.prompt: Stock of product P1 closed at 40 on Monday, 35 on Tuesday and 50 on Wednesday. A report adds the three figures. What does it return?
hints: A sum adds all three days.
Add Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.
The answer is the total of the three stock figures.
questions.onCorrect: The sum is 125, but there were never 125 units: each day's stock is largely the same units counted again.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the last day, not the sum. The report adds all three.
That is the average. The report adds the figures.

questions.prompt: Margin percentage is not additive across rows. Which name does this kind of measure carry? Answer with the one word or hyphenated name.
hints: Additive measures sum across every dimension, and semi-additive ones across all but time.
A percentage does not add up across any dimension.
questions.onCorrect: A percentage of this kind is a ratio, so it has to be rebuilt from additive parts such as revenue and cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Semi-additive measures, like balances, still add across some dimensions. A percentage adds across none.
Adding two margin percentages gives a number that is not any margin.

questions.prompt: Why is the average of 25% and 50% a poor margin for the two lines together?
hints: Compare the revenue of the two lines.

acceptedIdeas: It gives the small line the same weight as the large one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It gives the small line the same weight as the large one

questions.onCorrect: Each percentage divides by its own revenue, so adding the parts first and dividing once keeps the weights right.

misconceptions.feedback: SQL can average any number. The fault is in the meaning of the result.
Different costs are normal. The point is that each percentage is a ratio of different totals.
The size of a percentage does not stop it being averaged. The weights are the trouble.

choices.label: It gives the small line the same weight as the large one
Percentages cannot be averaged in SQL
The two lines have different costs
50% is too large to average

questions.prompt: Two sales lines sold 10 units for 300 in revenue and 5 units for 100 in revenue. What is the overall average unit price, as total revenue divided by total quantity, to two decimal places?
hints: Sum the additive parts first.
Total revenue over total quantity.
400 divided by 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue is 300 + 100 = 400 and quantity is 10 + 5 = 15, so 400 / 15 = 26.67.

questions.onCorrect: Unit price is rebuilt from two additive measures, which is why the fact table stores revenue and quantity.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two prices, 30 and 20, and gives the five-unit line the same weight as the ten-unit one.
That is the total revenue. The price is revenue divided by quantity.

questions.prompt: A table holds one row per product per day, giving the stock level at close. Which type of fact table is it?
hints: The row exists for every day, whether or not anything happened.
Look at the state, not the event.
questions.onCorrect: A periodic snapshot records state at regular intervals, which suits levels such as stock and balances.

misconceptions.feedback: A transaction fact records events. A day with no sales would have no row, so stock could not be read from it.

questions.prompt: The shop system has customers 17 and 18, and the web system has customers 17 and 40. Each system numbers its own customers, so all four are different people. How many rows does dim_customer hold?
hints: Count people, not ids.
Each system numbers its own customers.
Four customers means four rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four different people give four rows, each with its own surrogate key.

questions.onCorrect: A surrogate key lets the two 17s coexist, since the warehouse numbers rows itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the distinct source ids, 17, 18 and 40, but the two 17s are different people.
That counts one system only. Both systems feed the dimension.

questions.prompt: An accumulating snapshot tracks orders through ordered, paid, shipped and delivered. Three orders have each passed all four milestones. How many rows does the table hold?
hints: Check the grain: what does one row stand for?
One row stands for one order.
Count the orders, not the milestones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One row per order, updated at each milestone: 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The row keeps changing as the order progresses, which is what separates it from a transaction fact.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one row per milestone. The grain is one row per order, which is updated.
That counts the milestones. The rows are orders.

questions.prompt: Which measure is semi-additive?
hints: Which of these is a level at a moment, not an amount of activity?
questions.onCorrect: A balance adds across accounts on one day, but adding it across days gives a figure that means nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: Quantity sold adds across every dimension, time included.
Unit price is a ratio and does not add across any dimension.
Margin percentage is a ratio and does not add across any dimension.

choices.label: Quantity sold
Account balance
Unit price
Margin percentage

questions.prompt: An account's balance was 100 on Monday, 120 on Tuesday and 90 on Wednesday. What is its balance for the period, taking the end-of-period value?
hints: End of period means the last day.
Read off Wednesday.
Do not add or average the three days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The end-of-period value is the last day's balance, 90.

questions.onCorrect: For a balance the end-of-period value is 90, the average would be 103.33, and the sum of 310 means nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three days, which a balance does not allow.
That is the average, not the end-of-period value.

questions.prompt: Which fact table type has one row per order, updated as the order moves through paid, shipped and delivered?
hints: The row is revisited as milestones are reached.
The name says the row accumulates dates.
questions.onCorrect: The row is created when the order is placed and filled in as each milestone arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: A transaction fact is added once and not revisited.
A periodic snapshot adds a row each period instead of updating one.

questions.prompt: Representative R1 sold 40 on 10 January and 60 on 14 February, then moved from North to South on 1 March and sold 25 on 5 April. R2 sold 30 in the North on 6 April. The region column is overwritten, so R1 reads South. What total does a report by region show for North?
hints: After the overwrite, which sales belong to someone in the North?
R1 now reads South.
Only the sales of reps still marked North count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only R2 is still in the North, so North shows 30, instead of the 130 it really sold.

questions.onCorrect: Overwriting moved R1's January and February sales to South, so North now reports only R2's 30.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the North really sold, which a table with the old value gone cannot show.
That adds R1's two North sales only. After the overwrite they sit under South.

questions.prompt: Under a Type 2 design, how many rows does dim_rep hold for R1 once R1 has moved from North to South?
hints: A design that keeps every version holds one row per version.
Count the versions of R1.
North is one version and South is another.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One row for the North version and one for the South version: 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: Each change adds a row with its own surrogate key and validity dates, so history is kept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Type 1, where the old row is overwritten.
Only two versions exist, North and South.

questions.prompt: A sale is made on exactly 2026-03-01. The North row runs from 2025-01-01 to 2026-03-01 and the South row from 2026-03-01 to 9999-12-31. With valid_from included and valid_to excluded, how many rows does the sale match?
hints: Test the date against each row's range.
The end date of the North row is excluded.
Only one range contains the date.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2026-03-01 is not before the North row's end, but is on the South row's start, so only South matches: 1 row.

questions.onCorrect: Excluding the end date lets one row end on the day the next begins without overlap.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the end date as included, which makes the ranges overlap.
The South row starts on that date and includes it.

questions.prompt: Why does the April sale of 25 go to the South row?
hints: Compare the date with each row's range.

acceptedIdeas: 5 April lies in the half-open range that starts on 1 March
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 5 April lies in the half-open range that starts on 1 March

questions.onCorrect: The sale date must be on or after valid_from and before valid_to, and only one row satisfies both.

misconceptions.feedback: The key plays no part. The date range decides.
That is true of the present, but the join uses the date of the sale, so an April sale and a later-moved rep would differ.
The join does not pick the newest row; a February sale would find the North row.

choices.label: 5 April lies in the half-open range that starts on 1 March
The South row has the highest key
South is the current region of R1
April sales always go to the newest row

questions.prompt: Representative R3 was in West until 2026-02-01 and in East from that date on, with valid_to excluded. R3 sold 10 on 2026-01-05, 20 on 2026-02-01 and 35 on 2026-03-15. R4 is always in East and sold 5 on 2026-03-20. What is East's total in an as-of join?
hints: Decide for each sale which row its date falls in.
2026-02-01 belongs to the East row.
Add the East sales: R3's later two and R4's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sale of 10 is in West. 20, 35 and 5 fall in East: 20 + 35 + 5 = 60.

questions.onCorrect: The sale on the change date belongs to the new version, and the January sale stays with West.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the sale on 2026-02-01, which is on the East row's first day and so belongs to it.
That includes the sale of 10 from January, which was made while R3 was in West.

questions.prompt: A sales fact table and a returns fact table both join the same dim_product, with the same keys and meaning. What is such a shared dimension called?
hints: The word describes dimensions that agree across fact tables.
It starts with "conform".
questions.onCorrect: Because both facts use identical product keys, sales and returns can be compared by product.

misconceptions.feedback: A surrogate key identifies a row. The shared dimension as a whole is something else.

questions.prompt: A customer's phone number was keyed wrongly and has been corrected. Nobody needs the wrong number, so history is not wanted. Which Slowly Changing Dimension type fits? Answer with the type number, 1 or 2.
hints: Does anyone want to see the wrong number later?
Type 2 is for changes that really happened.
An error is corrected, not versioned.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The old value was an error, so overwriting it, Type 1, loses nothing that matters.

questions.onCorrect: Type 1 suits corrections, whereas Type 2 suits changes that really happened and still matter to past facts.

misconceptions.feedback: Type 2 would keep the wrong number as a version, which no report wants.

questions.prompt: Setup: CREATE TABLE dim_customer(sk INT, cust_id TEXT, city TEXT, valid_from TEXT, valid_to TEXT); INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (1,'C1','Leeds','2025-01-01','2026-03-01'),(2,'C1','York','2026-03-01','9999-12-31'),(3,'C2','Leeds','2025-01-01','9999-12-31'); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT,cust_id TEXT,sale_date TEXT,amount INT); INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'C1','2026-01-15',50),(2,'C1','2026-02-20',30),(3,'C1','2026-04-02',70),(4,'C2','2026-04-03',20); Join sales to dim_customer on cust_id with sale_date >= valid_from AND sale_date < valid_to. What is the York total?
hints: Match each sale to the row whose range holds its date.
C1's first two sales are before 2026-03-01.
Add the sales that land on a York row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the sale of 70 on 2026-04-02 falls in the York row, which starts on 2026-03-01: 70.

questions.onCorrect: The as-of join sends each sale to the version valid on its date, so only the April sale counts as York.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the York total for a join to current rows only. Here each sale uses the row valid on its date.
That is the Leeds total.

questions.prompt: With the same tables, join only to the current rows (valid_to = '9999-12-31'). What is the York total?
hints: Which row is current for C1?
Every C1 sale joins to that one row.
Add C1's three sales.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: C1's current row is York, so all three of C1's sales, 50 + 30 + 70, land on it: 150.

questions.onCorrect: Joining to current rows only puts every past sale under the present attribute, which is the error Type 2 prevents.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the as-of total. Here every C1 sale joins to the current York row.
That is the Leeds total under a current-row join.

questions.prompt: Finance must report each past sale under the sales region the account manager belonged to at the time. Which approach?
hints: The past must stay readable.

acceptedIdeas: Type 2: keep a row per version with validity dates
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Type 2: keep a row per version with validity dates

questions.onCorrect: Type 2 keeps every version with its dates, so each sale joins to the region valid on its date.

misconceptions.feedback: Overwriting loses the region each sale was made under.
Deleting the old rows loses the past regions entirely.
A region held only in the report cannot be tied to the date of each sale.

choices.label: Type 1: overwrite the region
Type 2: keep a row per version with validity dates
Delete the old rows
Store the region only in the report

questions.prompt: Invoice 1 has total 90 and 3 lines, invoice 2 has total 150 and 2 lines, and invoice 3 has total 40 and 1 line. Each invoice is joined to its lines and the invoice total is summed. What does SUM(total) return?
hints: After the join, how many rows does each invoice occupy?
Multiply each total by its line count.
questions.onCorrect: Each invoice total is repeated once per line, so the join multiplies it before the sum.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the invoices alone. After the join each invoice appears once per line.
That counts the joined rows. The column being summed is the total.

questions.prompt: The three invoices have 3, 2 and 1 lines. How many rows does the join of invoices to invoice lines return?
hints: A join on a one-to-many key gives one row per child.
Add the line counts.
Compare the result with the 3 invoices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The join returns one row per line, so 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 rows, while invoices has 3.

questions.onCorrect: When the row count after a join is larger than the parent table, the parent rows have been repeated.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of invoices. The join returns one row for each matching line.
That multiplies the counts. A join of this kind returns one row per child row.

questions.prompt: Why does aggregating the lines to one row per invoice before the join keep the total right?
hints: Think about how many rows each invoice matches after the lines are aggregated.

acceptedIdeas: Each invoice then matches exactly one row, so it is not repeated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each invoice then matches exactly one row, so it is not repeated

questions.onCorrect: A join that matches each parent to one child row cannot repeat the parent.

misconceptions.feedback: The join still runs, but on a child table that has one row per invoice.
SUM adds every row it is given, repeated or not.
The invoice total is read from invoices as before; nothing is recalculated.

choices.label: Each invoice then matches exactly one row, so it is not repeated
The join is skipped
SUM ignores repeated rows
The invoice total is recalculated from the lines

questions.prompt: Orders 1, 2 and 3 have totals of 80, 120 and 50 and are joined to payments that have been aggregated to one row per order. What does SUM(total) over the joined result return?
hints: After aggregation each order matches one row.
Nothing is repeated.
Add the three totals.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With one payment row per order each order is matched once, so the sum is 80 + 120 + 50 = 250.

questions.onCorrect: Aggregating the many side to the parent's grain first is the standard repair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum when payments are not aggregated: 80 × 2 + 120 × 1 + 50 × 4.
