That counts the orders. The column holds their totals.

questions.prompt: A data scientist wants one flat table, with every order, customer and product column on one row, to feed a single modelling tool. Which shape is that? Answer with its usual name.
hints: It trades repeated data for having no joins.
The shape puts everything on every row.
questions.onCorrect: A wide table suits one purpose well, but it repeats data and hides the grain, so it is built last from a star.

misconceptions.feedback: A star keeps the dimensions in separate tables, so it needs joins.

questions.prompt: A data vault holds two hubs, customer and product, one link between them for order lines, and one satellite for each hub. How many tables is that in all?
hints: Count hubs, links and satellites separately.
Two hubs and one link make three.
Add the two satellites.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 hubs + 1 link + 2 satellites = 5 tables.

questions.onCorrect: A vault has more tables than the star built from it, which is the price of its auditability.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts hubs and the link but leaves out the satellites.
That leaves out one of the satellites, or counts one hub too few.

questions.prompt: Customer 1 has a credit limit of 500 and 3 orders, and customer 2 has a limit of 800 and 2 orders. The customers are joined to their orders and the credit limit is summed. What does SUM(credit_limit) return?
hints: The measure belongs to the customer, not the order.
Multiply each limit by its order count.
Add the two products.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 × 3 + 800 × 2 = 1,500 + 1,600 = 3,100, against 1,300 for the customers alone.

questions.onCorrect: Any customer attribute, not only money, is repeated once per order after the join.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum on customers alone. After the join each limit repeats once per order.
That counts the orders. The column holds credit limits.

questions.prompt: Setup: CREATE TABLE o(id INT, total INT); INSERT INTO o VALUES (1,100),(2,200),(3,300); CREATE TABLE i(oid INT, sku TEXT); INSERT INTO i VALUES (1,'a'),(1,'b'),(2,'c'),(3,'a'),(3,'b'),(3,'c'); What does SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM o JOIN i ON i.oid = o.id return?
hints: Count the items of each order in i.
Each total repeats once per item.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 1, 2 and 3 have 2, 1 and 3 items, so the sum is 100 × 2 + 200 × 1 + 300 × 3 = 1,300.

questions.onCorrect: The join has six rows, one per item, and each carries its order's total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum on o alone. After the join each order repeats once per item.
That is the number of joined rows.

questions.prompt: With the same tables, what does SELECT SUM(total) FROM o return?
hints: No join this time.
Each order appears once.
Add the three totals.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sum is over o alone, with one row per order: 100 + 200 + 300 = 600.

questions.onCorrect: Summing at the grain of o, before any join to i, avoids the repetition.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum after joining to i, where totals repeat.
That counts items, not totals.

questions.prompt: Which shape fits integrating ten source systems with full audit history before building reports?
hints: Integration and reporting need different shapes.
questions.onCorrect: The vault integrates and keeps history, and the dimensional marts built on it serve reporting.

misconceptions.feedback: A wide table hides the source of each value and cannot keep audit history.
A spreadsheet cannot integrate ten systems with history.
Normalised tables alone leave every report to chain joins and give no layer for audit.

choices.label: One big table
Data vault feeding dimensional marts
A single spreadsheet
Normalised tables only, no marts

questions.prompt: Seven models each read the table raw.orders directly by its name and each renames its columns in its own way. The source table is then renamed raw.orders_v2. How many models have to be edited?
hints: Which models contain the old table name?
Each of them reads it directly.
Count the models.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every model names the table, so each of the seven has to be edited.

questions.onCorrect: Seven edits, and seven renaming conventions to keep consistent, which is what a staging layer removes.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be so if only one model read the table. Here all seven do.
The models do not notice the rename on their own. Each one still names the old table.

questions.prompt: A model joins stg_orders to stg_customers to give one row per order with the customer's name. Which layer is it in? Answer with the layer name.
hints: It reshapes data from staging models and is not the finished table.
It is neither the first step nor the last.
questions.onCorrect: Intermediate models join and reshape, and the marts that read them are the finished tables.

misconceptions.feedback: A staging model reads one source and changes nothing but names and types. Joining belongs one layer later.
A mart is the finished table for use. This join is a step on the way to one.

questions.prompt: A model has 2,000,000,000 rows and gains 5,000,000 new ones each hour. How many times more rows does a full rebuild process in an hour than an incremental run that handles only the new rows?
hints: Divide the size of the table by the size of an hourly batch.
Cancel six zeros from each.
questions.onCorrect: The saving grows with the table: the full rebuild repeats work on rows that cannot have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio the other way round, the incremental run over the full rebuild.
Check the zeros: 2,000,000,000 has nine and 5,000,000 has six, so the quotient has three digits.

questions.prompt: In the graph, how many models, counting only models and not the raw sources, must be built before fct_orders can run?
hints: Start from fct_orders and go back along the arrows.
Its two direct parents are intermediate models.
Add the staging models they read.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: fct_orders reads int_orders_joined and int_payments_by_order, which read stg_customers, stg_orders and stg_payments: 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The tool follows the arrows back from a model to work out everything that must run first.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only its direct parents. Their own parents must run first too.
That counts every model. dim_customers and rpt_daily_revenue are not needed.

questions.prompt: Why can stg_orders and stg_payments be built in the same round?
hints: What would stop one running before the other?
questions.onCorrect: Models that have no path between them can run in any order, so the tool can run them together.

misconceptions.feedback: Being a view does not decide order. A view can depend on another model.
The layer does not decide it. Dependence does.
The columns play no part. The arrows decide.

choices.label: Neither depends on the other
Both are views
Both are in the staging layer
They have the same number of columns

questions.prompt: A new model, int_refunds, reads stg_payments and feeds fct_orders. Besides it, fct_orders still reads what it did before. How many models must now run before fct_orders?
hints: Start from the five that ran before.
int_refunds is one new model.
stg_payments was already counted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The earlier five plus int_refunds make 6.

questions.onCorrect: A new model adds only the models that are not already upstream, and stg_payments was.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before int_refunds was added.
int_refunds reads stg_payments, which is already counted, so only one model is added.

questions.prompt: If stg_customers changes, how many models downstream of it, directly or indirectly, have to be rebuilt?
hints: Follow the arrows forward from stg_customers.
Two models read it directly.
Add the models that read those.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: int_orders_joined and dim_customers read it, fct_orders reads the first, and rpt_daily_revenue reads that: 4.

questions.onCorrect: The same graph answers both questions, what must run first and what is affected, which is the idea behind lineage.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only its direct children. Their children are affected too.
That leaves out rpt_daily_revenue, which reads fct_orders.

questions.prompt: Where should casting amount from text to a decimal and renaming orderid to order_id happen? Name the layer.
hints: Which layer mirrors one source and changes only names and types?
Doing it once, early, means every model after it sees the same clean columns.
questions.onCorrect: Staging models mirror one source each, so every later model sees the same cleaned columns.

misconceptions.feedback: A mart is the finished table. Casting there means every other model has to repeat it.

questions.prompt: A model with several billion rows grows by appending new events each hour. Which materialisation suits it? Answer in one or two words.
hints: The table is large and only gains new rows.
Rebuilding every row each hour repeats work on rows that cannot change.
questions.onCorrect: An incremental table adds only the new rows each run, so the cost follows the new data and not the whole table.

misconceptions.feedback: A view would re-run the whole query on every read, over billions of rows.
A plain table would be rebuilt in full every hour.
An ephemeral model is never stored, so billions of rows would be recomputed in each model that used it.

questions.prompt: In dbt, which function does one model use to refer to another so that the tool can order the build? Give the function name.
hints: It takes the name of the model as its argument.
It is a function that takes a model name and gives back the table to read.
questions.onCorrect: The tool reads every ref call to build the graph, so the order and the lineage come from the code itself.

misconceptions.feedback: The source function points at raw tables outside the project, not at other models.

questions.prompt: A target holds three invoices, and the latest updated_at in it is 2026-06-10. The source holds six: id 1 on 06-08, id 2 on 06-11, id 3 on 06-10, id 4 on 06-09, id 5 on 06-11 and id 6 on 06-12. A run reads only rows with updated_at later than the latest in the target. How many source rows does it read?
hints: Compare each date with 2026-06-10.
Strictly later excludes 06-10 itself.
Count ids 2, 5 and 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only ids 2, 5 and 6 have an updated_at after 2026-06-10: 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: Three rows pass, of which one is a changed row and two are new, and the other three rows are skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the whole source, which is a full rebuild.
One of those is stamped on the cut-off date itself, and the filter is strictly later than that date.

questions.prompt: The run reads ids 2, 5 and 6 and merges them into the target by id. Id 2 already exists there, and ids 5 and 6 do not. How many rows does the target hold afterwards?
hints: An existing id is updated, not added again.
Two ids are new.
Add them to the three that were there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 2 is updated in place and ids 5 and 6 are added, so 3 + 2 = 5 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The merge is by key, so a changed row replaces its old version and new ones are added.

misconceptions.feedback: Id 4 was not read, so it is not in the target.
That is the target before the run. Two new ids are added.

questions.prompt: Which source id is never loaded by the filter, although it is in the source? Give the id.
hints: Look for a source row that is not in the target.
It must have a timestamp older than the cut-off.
Only one such row exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 4 is stamped 2026-06-09, earlier than the target's latest 2026-06-10, so the filter skips it, and it was never loaded.

questions.onCorrect: The filter assumes that new rows carry new timestamps, and a row that arrives late carries an old one.

misconceptions.feedback: Id 1 is already in the target, so it is not missing.
Id 3 is in the target already.

questions.prompt: Why does re-reading id 3 with a lookback not create a duplicate row?
hints: What does the merge compare to decide a row already exists?

acceptedIdeas: The merge matches on the unique key and updates the row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The merge matches on the unique key and updates the row

questions.onCorrect: A unique key lets a re-read row replace itself, which is what makes a lookback safe.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing removes rows first. The merge replaces the matching row.
Id 3 is read, and the merge matches it by key. The data being unchanged is not why.
The filter does not look at the target's rows, only its latest timestamp.

choices.label: The merge matches on the unique key and updates the row
The target removes old rows first
Id 3 is ignored because it is unchanged
The filter removes rows that are already loaded

questions.prompt: With a lookback of 1 day the filter reads rows with updated_at later than 2026-06-09. How many of the six source rows does it read?
hints: Compare each date with 2026-06-09.
Strictly later excludes 06-09.
Count ids 2, 3, 5 and 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ids 2, 3, 5 and 6 are later than 06-09. Id 4 is stamped 06-09 exactly and is left out: 4 rows.

questions.onCorrect: A lookback of 1 day still misses the late row, because its timestamp falls on the cut-off, and the window must be longer than the lateness.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the late row, but its date is not later than the cut-off.
Id 3, stamped 06-10, is later than 06-09 and is read.

questions.prompt: A model definition is changed so that amounts are stored in cents. The target has 6 rows, and the next incremental run reads and rewrites 3 rows. How many rows still hold amounts in the old unit?
hints: Which rows does an incremental run touch?
Only those it reads.
Subtract them from the 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the 3 rows that are read follow the new logic, so 6 − 3 = 3 rows keep the old one.

questions.onCorrect: Changing the definition does not change old rows. A full refresh is what rebuilds them under the new logic.

misconceptions.feedback: An incremental run does not rewrite rows it does not read.
The rows that are read are rewritten with the new logic.

questions.prompt: A row stamped 2026-06-09 reaches the source after the target's latest updated_at has already reached 2026-06-12. The filter reads rows with updated_at later than the latest minus N days. What is the smallest whole number N that reads the row?
hints: The row must be strictly later than the cut-off.
Work out the cut-off for N = 3.
Try the next whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 06-12 minus N days must be earlier than 06-09. N = 3 gives 06-09, which is not earlier, so N = 4.

questions.onCorrect: A strict comparison needs a window one day longer than the lateness, which is why a lookback is chosen with some margin.

misconceptions.feedback: N = 3 gives a cut-off of 06-09, and the row is stamped 06-09, which is not later.
That gives a cut-off of 06-10, which is later than the row.

questions.prompt: Setup: CREATE TABLE tgt(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT, updated_at TEXT); INSERT INTO tgt VALUES (1,10,'2026-05-01'),(2,20,'2026-05-02'),(3,30,'2026-05-03'); CREATE TABLE src(id INT, v INT, updated_at TEXT); INSERT INTO src VALUES (1,10,'2026-05-01'),(2,25,'2026-05-04'),(3,30,'2026-05-03'),(4,40,'2026-05-04'),(5,50,'2026-05-02'); Merge rows with updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM tgt) into tgt by id. How many rows does tgt hold afterwards?
hints: Find the latest updated_at in tgt.
Read the source rows later than that.
One id updates an existing row and one adds a new row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The filter reads ids 2 and 4. Id 2 replaces its old row and id 4 is added, so tgt holds ids 1, 2, 3 and 4: 4 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The filter reads ids 2 and 4, and the merge updates one row and adds one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts id 5, which is stamped 05-02, earlier than the latest in tgt, so it is not read.
That is tgt before the run. One more row is added.

questions.prompt: Which source id is never loaded by that filter? Give the id.
hints: Look for a source row that is not in tgt.
Its timestamp must be older than the target's latest.
Only one such row exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 5 is stamped 2026-05-02, which is earlier than the target's latest, 2026-05-03, so the filter never reads it.

questions.onCorrect: A row with an old timestamp that appears after the target has moved on is skipped for good.

misconceptions.feedback: That row is later than the target's latest, so it is read.
Id 1 is already in the target.

questions.prompt: Which technique, re-reading a recent window of rows and merging them on the unique key, picks up late-arriving rows? Answer in one or two words.
hints: The window reaches back from the latest timestamp.
It is named for looking back over recent rows.
questions.onCorrect: A lookback re-reads recent rows, and the unique key keeps the re-read from duplicating them.

misconceptions.feedback: A full refresh rebuilds everything, which also catches late rows but costs the whole build.

questions.prompt: Seven employees have these emails: ana, bo, missing, bo, eli, fay and missing. A unique test returns one row for each email value that appears more than once, ignoring missing values. How many rows does it return?
hints: Which email appears more than once?
Missing values are not counted as values.
Count the repeated values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only bo appears twice. The two missing values are ignored, so one row is returned.

questions.onCorrect: The unique test returns the repeated values, one row each, and leaves missing values to a not_null test.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the missing values as a repeated value. A not_null test handles them, and the unique test ignores them.
Bo appears twice, so the test does return a row.

questions.prompt: How many rows does a not_null test on email return for the seven employees?
hints: The test returns rows where the value is missing.
Look for missing emails.
Count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The test returns the rows whose email is missing: employees 3 and 7, so 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: A not_null test returns the offending rows themselves, so you can see which employees lack an email.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the repeated email. A not_null test looks for missing values.
That adds the repeated email. The test returns only the rows with a missing email.

questions.prompt: The departments table holds ids 10, 20 and 30. Employee 6 has dept_id 99 and employee 5 has a missing dept_id. How many rows does a relationships test on dept_id return?
hints: Which dept_ids are not in departments?
A missing value does not point at anything.
Count the ones that point at a missing department.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Employee 6 points at a department that does not exist. Employee 5 has no dept_id, so it is not a broken reference: 1 row.

questions.onCorrect: A relationships test returns rows that point at a parent that is not there, and it skips missing keys.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the missing dept_id as a broken reference. A missing value points at nothing, so a not_null test is the one to catch it.
Employee 6 has dept_id 99, which is not in departments.

questions.prompt: Why does the relationships test leave out rows whose dept_id is missing?
hints: Is a reference that was never made a broken reference?

acceptedIdeas: A missing value points at no parent, so no reference is broken
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A missing value points at no parent, so no reference is broken

questions.onCorrect: Whether a key may be missing is a separate rule, which a not_null test states.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing value equals nothing, not everything.
The join can read it, but a missing key matches no row, which is why the filter is added.
The test checks every row.

choices.label: A missing value points at no parent, so no reference is broken
NULL equals every department
The join cannot read NULL
The test only checks the first row

questions.prompt: Orders have the statuses paid, paid, shipped, refunded, paid, void and paid. An accepted_values test allows paid and shipped only. How many rows does it return?
hints: Mark each status that is not on the list.
Refunded is not allowed here.
Count the orders with a status that is not allowed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Refunded and void are not on the list, so the test returns those 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The allowed list is part of the test, so shortening it makes more rows fail.

misconceptions.feedback: That finds only one of them. Neither refunded nor void is allowed.
That counts the paid rows, which are allowed.

questions.prompt: Orders arrive from a source with the column orderid. After the staging model renames it to order_id, where is the best place to put a unique test on order_id? Name the layer.
hints: Where is the key first given its final name?
A failure there is closest to the source.
questions.onCorrect: In staging a duplicate key is a fact about the source, so the failing rows point straight at the cause.

misconceptions.feedback: By the mart a duplicate key may have been multiplied by joins, and the cause is several models away.

questions.prompt: A business rule says the ship date must not be before the order date. Orders: 1 ordered 05-01, shipped 05-03; 2 ordered 05-04, shipped 05-02; 3 ordered 05-05, shipped 05-05; 4 ordered 05-06, shipped 05-04. How many rows does a test of this rule return?
hints: The test returns rows where shipped is earlier than ordered.
Compare each pair of dates.
Equal dates are allowed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 2 and 4 were shipped before they were ordered: 2 rows. Order 3 shipped on the order date, which the rule allows.

questions.onCorrect: A custom rule is tested the same way as the standard four: write the query that returns the violations.

misconceptions.feedback: Order 4 also breaks the rule, as it shipped before it was ordered.
Order 3 shipped on the order date, and the rule only forbids shipping before it.

questions.prompt: Setup: CREATE TABLE customers(id INT, email TEXT); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,NULL),(3,'a@x.com'),(4,'d@x.com'),(5,NULL); CREATE TABLE orders(id INT, customer_id INT, status TEXT); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,'paid'),(11,2,'paid'),(12,9,'shipped'),(13,3,'refunded'),(14,NULL,'paid'),(15,4,'void'),(16,12,'paid'); Write the relationships test: orders whose non-null customer_id has no matching customers.id. What is the sum of the order ids it returns?
hints: Find the customer_ids that are not in customers and are not missing.
Two orders qualify.
Add their ids.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 12 (customer 9) and 16 (customer 12) have no matching customer, and 12 + 16 = 28. Order 14 has no customer_id, so it is ignored.

questions.onCorrect: The test returns orders 12 and 16, and skips order 14 because its customer_id is missing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only one of the returned ids.
That includes order 14, whose customer_id is missing, so it is not a broken reference.

questions.prompt: With the same customers table, how many rows does a not_null test on email return?
hints: The test returns rows with a missing value.
Look at the email column.
Count the missing ones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customers 2 and 5 have a missing email, so the test returns 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The not_null test returns rows, not a count, so you would see customers 2 and 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the repeated email, which is for a unique test.
That includes a customer whose email is present.

questions.prompt: With the same orders table, which order id fails an accepted_values test for status in ('paid', 'shipped', 'refunded')? Give the id.
hints: Find the status that is not on the list.
Only one order has it.
questions.onCorrect: Order 15 has the status void, which is not allowed, so it is the only row returned.

questions.prompt: East has revenue 300 from 5 orders and West has revenue 900 from 45 orders. What is the average order value over both regions together?
hints: Combine the regions before dividing.
Add the revenues and add the orders.
Divide the total revenue by the total orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total revenue is 300 + 900 = 1,200 and total orders are 5 + 45 = 50, so 1,200 / 50 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: An average order value for the whole business is total revenue over total orders, whatever the regions hold.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two regional values, 60 and 20, and treats the two regions as equal in size.
That is the total revenue. The value is revenue per order.

questions.prompt: The agreed definition of revenue is the sum of order amounts excluding cancelled orders. In January the orders were paid 420, shipped 260 and cancelled 90. What is January revenue by that definition?
hints: Which statuses does the definition exclude?
Leave out the cancelled orders.
Add the paid and the shipped amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Cancelled orders are excluded, so revenue is 420 + 260 = 680.

questions.onCorrect: A metric carries its filter with it, which is how every dashboard comes to apply the same one.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the cancelled orders, which the definition excludes.
That is only the shipped orders. Paid orders count as well.

questions.prompt: North has revenue 200 from 10 orders and South has revenue 1,000 from 20 orders. What is the overall average order value?
hints: Add the revenues and the orders first.
Total revenue is 1,200 and total orders are 30.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The ratio is formed after the parts are added, so each region weighs in by its number of orders.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two regional values, 20 and 50.
That is total revenue, not revenue per order.

questions.prompt: Why is the average of two regional averages not the overall average?
hints: Compare the number of orders behind each average.

acceptedIdeas: Each regional average rests on a different number of orders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each regional average rests on a different number of orders

questions.onCorrect: A ratio of sums gives each order the same weight, whereas an average of ratios gives each region the same weight.

misconceptions.feedback: Averages can be averaged, but the result ignores how much data stands behind each.
The question does not involve currency.
Revenue can be divided by orders. The issue is the order of operations.

choices.label: Each regional average rests on a different number of orders
Averages cannot be added
The regions use different currencies
Division is not allowed on revenue

questions.prompt: Monthly revenue is 100 in January, 150 in February and 120 in March. What is the cumulative revenue at the end of March?
hints: Cumulative means a running total.
Add January, February and March.
Add 100 to 150 and then 120.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cumulative metric adds the months so far: 100 + 150 + 120 = 370.

questions.onCorrect: A cumulative metric is a simple metric accumulated over time, so it adds months where a ratio would divide.

misconceptions.feedback: That is March alone. A cumulative metric accumulates from the start.
That stops at February. March is included.

questions.prompt: Segment A has customers 1, 2, 3 and 4, segment B has 3, 4 and 5, and segment C has 4 and 6. How many distinct customers are there in all?
hints: List every id that appears in any segment.
Count each id once.
Write the ids in order and cross out repeats.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distinct ids are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6: 6 customers, although the segment counts add up to 9.

questions.onCorrect: A distinct count must be recomputed over the union of the groups, because it cannot be got by adding.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three segment counts, and counts customers 3 and 4 more than once.
That misses a customer who is only in segment C.

questions.prompt: North has revenue 700 and 4 distinct customers. South has revenue 300 and 3 distinct customers. Two customers are in both regions. What is the overall revenue per distinct customer?
hints: Revenue can be added across regions, distinct customers cannot.
Take the shared customers off the sum of the counts once.
Divide 1,000 by the distinct customers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue is 700 + 300 = 1,000. Distinct customers are 4 + 3 − 2 = 5. Revenue per customer is 1,000 / 5 = 200.

questions.onCorrect: A ratio built from a non-additive part needs both parts recomputed over the whole group.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two regional values, 175 and 100.
That divides by 7, the sum of the regional counts, which counts the shared customers twice.

questions.prompt: Region A has revenue 100 from 10 orders and region B has revenue 900 from 30 orders. What is the overall average order value?
hints: Add the revenues and add the orders.
Total revenue is 1,000.
Divide by the total number of orders.
questions.onCorrect: The overall value is a ratio of totals, so the larger region counts for more.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two regional values, 10 and 30.
That is the total revenue.

questions.prompt: Region A's customers are 1, 2 and 3, and region B's are 3 and 4. How many distinct customers are there overall?
hints: List the ids in either region.
Count each id once.
Customer 3 appears in both.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ids are 1, 2, 3 and 4. Customer 3 is in both regions, so the sum of 5 counts one customer twice.

questions.onCorrect: A distinct count over the whole group is not the sum of the group counts.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the regional counts, 3 and 2, and counts customer 3 twice.
That is the count in one region.

questions.prompt: Two dashboards show different revenue for the same month. Which layer defines revenue once so that every dashboard reuses it? Answer in two words.
hints: The layer sits between the models and the dashboards.
Its job is to define metrics and dimensions in one place.
questions.onCorrect: With one definition behind every dashboard, a change to it, such as a new filter, reaches all of them at once.

misconceptions.feedback: Each dashboard then keeps its own definition, which is the cause of the problem.

questions.prompt: Models are connected like this: crm to stg_crm; stg_crm to int_customer_orders; int_customer_orders to mart_revenue and mart_marketing; mart_revenue to dash_sales and dash_exec; mart_marketing to dash_exec. How many nodes are downstream of stg_crm, directly or through others?
hints: Follow the arrows forward from stg_crm.
Keep going until a node has no arrows leaving it.
Count each node once, even if two paths reach it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: int_customer_orders is one hop down, mart_revenue and mart_marketing two, dash_sales and dash_exec three: 5 nodes.

questions.onCorrect: Downstream means built from it at any distance, which is why a change near the start reaches so far.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the direct consumer. Everything built from that one is downstream as well.
That includes stg_crm itself, which is not downstream of itself.

questions.prompt: In the lineage graph in the figure, how many nodes are upstream of dash_exec?
hints: Follow the arrows backward from dash_exec.
It has two parents, and each has parents of its own.
Count every node on any path back to a source.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: dash_exec reads mart_revenue and mart_marketing, which lead back through int_customer_orders, stg_crm, stg_shop and stg_ads to crm, shop and ads: 9 nodes.

questions.onCorrect: Upstream is everything that the node depends on, back to the sources.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the two direct parents. Their own parents are upstream as well.
That misses one of the sources or staging models. Dash_exec depends on all three sources.

questions.prompt: If int_customer_orders changes its output, how many nodes in the graph are downstream of it and so may be affected?
hints: Follow the arrows forward from the model.
It feeds two marts.
Add the dashboards they feed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: mart_revenue and mart_marketing read it directly, and dash_sales and dash_exec read those: 4 nodes.

questions.onCorrect: The count is what a change has to be checked against, and it includes the dashboards that people see.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the two marts. The dashboards built from them are affected too.
That includes int_customer_orders itself.

questions.prompt: Why is the ads source not upstream of dash_sales?
hints: Follow the arrows back from dash_sales and see where they stop.

acceptedIdeas: No path of arrows leads from ads to dash_sales
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No path of arrows leads from ads to dash_sales

questions.onCorrect: Upstream is decided by paths. dash_sales reads only the revenue mart, which does not touch ads.

misconceptions.feedback: Layers do not decide it. Paths do: dash_exec is in the same layer as dash_sales and has ads upstream.
Sources are the most upstream nodes of all.
A dashboard has parents, which is how it is built.

choices.label: No path of arrows leads from ads to dash_sales
The two are in different layers
Ads is a source, and sources are never upstream
dash_sales is a dashboard, and dashboards have no parents

questions.prompt: Walk downstream from stg_ads. Its only consumer is mart_marketing, which feeds dash_exec. How many nodes are downstream of stg_ads?
hints: List the consumers of stg_ads.
Then list the consumers of those.
Count each once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: mart_marketing is one hop down and dash_exec is two: 2 nodes.

questions.onCorrect: The same walk, run forward from a node, gives its impact.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the direct consumer.
That includes stg_ads itself.

questions.prompt: In an OpenLineage run event, which field lists the datasets that a job reads? Answer with the field name.
hints: The event also has a field for the datasets the job writes.
The name is the plain word for what goes into a job.
questions.onCorrect: An event names the job, the run, the inputs and the outputs, and a lineage store joins the events into edges.

misconceptions.feedback: Outputs are the datasets a job writes. The ones it reads are listed in a different field.

questions.prompt: The mart_revenue table has 5 columns. Column-level lineage shows that 2 of them are computed from shop.amt, and the other 3 do not use it. If shop.amt is renamed, how many columns of mart_revenue are unaffected?
hints: Column-level lineage names the exact columns.
Subtract the affected columns from all of them.
5 minus the affected ones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 − 2 = 3 columns do not depend on shop.amt.

questions.onCorrect: Column-level lineage narrows a table-level warning to the columns that really use the changed one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number that are affected.
Table-level lineage flags every column, but column-level lineage shows which ones really depend on it.

questions.prompt: Edges: s1 to stg1; s2 to stg2; stg1 and stg2 to int1; int1 to mart1; stg2 to mart2; mart1 to d1 and d2; mart2 to d2. How many nodes are downstream of stg1?
hints: Follow the arrows forward from stg1.
int1 feeds mart1.
Mart1 feeds two dashboards.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: stg1 feeds int1, which feeds mart1, which feeds d1 and d2: int1, mart1, d1 and d2 make 4 nodes.

questions.onCorrect: Downstream of stg1 are int1, mart1, d1 and d2.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the direct consumer.
That leaves out one of the dashboards. Mart1 feeds two.

questions.prompt: In the same graph, how many nodes are upstream of d2?
hints: Follow the arrows backward from d2.
It has two parents, mart1 and mart2.
Go back until you reach the sources.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d2 reads mart1 and mart2, which lead back through int1, stg1 and stg2 to s1 and s2: 7 nodes.

questions.onCorrect: Upstream of d2 are mart1, mart2, int1, stg1, stg2, s1 and s2.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the two direct parents.
That misses the two sources.

questions.prompt: In the same graph, source s2 changes shape. How many dashboards (d1, d2) can be affected?
hints: Walk downstream from s2.
stg2 feeds int1 and mart2.
See which dashboards those reach.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: s2 feeds stg2, which feeds int1 and mart2. Mart1 reads int1 and feeds both dashboards, and mart2 feeds d2: 2 dashboards.

questions.onCorrect: A change to s2 reaches both dashboards by different routes, which is why impact analysis follows every path.

misconceptions.feedback: Mart1 feeds d1 and d2, and both are reached from stg2 through int1.
A dashboard is reached through the chain of models even though s2 is not connected directly.

questions.prompt: A table has 2,000 rows, and 1,840 of them have a postcode. What percentage of the rows are complete for postcode?
hints: Completeness is the rows with a value over all rows.
Divide 1,840 by 2,000.
Multiply the result by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Completeness is a rate, so it can be compared with a target and tracked over time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of rows that are missing a postcode, not the share that has one.
That is the count of complete rows. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: A table of people has a birth date in the year 2090. Which quality dimension does this break? Answer in one word.
hints: The value is present, and it is the only one for that person.
It breaks a rule about what dates are allowed.
questions.onCorrect: Validity checks values against rules such as formats and ranges, which needs no outside source.

misconceptions.feedback: Accuracy needs an outside reference, such as a record of when the person was really born. A future date breaks a rule that can be checked without one.
The value is present, so the row is complete. The fault is in the value itself.

questions.prompt: A table has 500 rows and 450 distinct order ids. What is the uniqueness of order_id, as a percentage?
hints: Uniqueness is distinct values over all rows.
Divide 450 by 500.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Uniqueness is the rate of distinct values, and a rate below 100% means some ids appear more than once.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of rows that repeat an id, not the share that is distinct.
That is the count of distinct ids. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: Daily row counts, in thousands, were 200, 220, 200 and 220, so the mean is 210 and the population standard deviation is 10. What is the z-score of today's count of 175?
hints: Subtract the mean from today's count.
Divide the difference by 10.
The count is below the mean, so the sign is negative.
questions.onCorrect: A z-score of −3.5 puts today's count more than three standard deviations below its recent mean, which is rare enough to investigate.

misconceptions.feedback: The count is below the mean, so the z-score is negative.
That is the distance from the mean. Divide it by the standard deviation.

questions.prompt: Why is a count compared with recent history and not with a fixed limit?
hints: Think about what happens to a fixed limit as the business grows.

acceptedIdeas: Volumes drift and have seasons, so what is normal changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Volumes drift and have seasons, so what is normal changes

questions.onCorrect: Comparing with a moving window lets the baseline follow growth and weekly patterns.

misconceptions.feedback: A fixed limit can be written in SQL. The problem is that it stops being right.
Recent history may be larger or smaller. The point is that it tracks the data.
Standard deviations are never negative, but that is not the reason.

choices.label: Volumes drift and have seasons, so what is normal changes
A fixed limit cannot be written in SQL
Recent history is always larger
Standard deviations cannot be negative

questions.prompt: Daily counts were 300, 340, 300 and 340, with a mean of 320 and a population standard deviation of 20. What is the z-score of today's count of 380?
hints: Subtract the mean from today's count.
Divide the difference by 20.
The count is above the mean.
questions.onCorrect: A z-score of 3 sits exactly on the usual alert line, so whether it is flagged depends on whether the rule is strict.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance from the mean. Divide it by the standard deviation.
The count is above the mean, so the z-score is positive.

questions.prompt: A table was last updated at 02:15 and it is now 09:00. Its freshness target is 4 hours. By how many hours is it in breach?
hints: Work out the age from 02:15 to 09:00.
The age is 6 hours and 45 minutes.
Subtract the target from the age.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Its age is 6 hours 45 minutes, or 6.75 hours. Against a 4-hour target the breach is 6.75 − 4 = 2.75 hours.

questions.onCorrect: A breach is measured as the excess over the target, which is how a service level is tracked.

misconceptions.feedback: That is its age. The breach is the part of the age beyond the target.
The age from 02:15 to 09:00 is 6 hours 45 minutes, not 6 hours 15.

questions.prompt: Weekday counts average 210, but Saturdays are quiet. The last four Saturdays had counts of 80, 100, 80 and 100, with a mean of 90 and a population standard deviation of 10. This Saturday has 120. What is its z-score against the Saturdays?
hints: Use the Saturday history, not the weekday mean.
Subtract 90 from 120.
Divide by 10.
questions.onCorrect: Comparing like with like, here Saturdays with Saturdays, keeps a normal weekly pattern from looking like an anomaly.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares with the weekday mean of 210, which is the wrong baseline for a Saturday.
That is the distance from the mean. Divide it by the standard deviation.

questions.prompt: 940 of 1,000 rows have a non-null email. What is the completeness, in percent?
hints: Divide complete rows by all rows.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Completeness counts only non-null values, so a blank or null email makes the row incomplete.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that is missing.
That is the count, not the percentage.

questions.prompt: Daily row counts (thousands) were 95, 105, 95 and 105. Using the population standard deviation, what is the z-score of today's count of 85?
hints: Find the mean of the four counts.
The standard deviation is 5.
(85 minus the mean) divided by 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 100 and the standard deviation is 5, so (85 − 100) / 5 = −3.

questions.onCorrect: A z-score of −3 marks a count three standard deviations below the recent mean.

misconceptions.feedback: The count is below the mean, so the z-score is negative.
That is the distance from the mean. Divide it by the standard deviation.

questions.prompt: A table was last updated at 03:00 and it is 09:00. Its freshness target is 4 hours. By how many hours is it in breach?
hints: Work out the age first.
From 03:00 to 09:00 is 6 hours.
Subtract the target from the age.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The age is 6 hours. Against the 4-hour target it exceeds it by 2 hours.

questions.onCorrect: The table is 2 hours past the point where it should have been refreshed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the age of the table. The breach is the excess over the target.
That is the target.

questions.prompt: Four reports read the orders table. Three of them select the column order_total by name, and one reads only order_id. The producer renames order_total to total. How many reports fail on the next run?
hints: Which reports name order_total?
The rename removes the old name.
Count the reports that name it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three that select order_total by name no longer find it. The one that reads only order_id is unaffected: 3 reports.

questions.onCorrect: A rename is a removal as far as a consumer is concerned, and each consumer finds out when its query fails.

misconceptions.feedback: The report that reads only order_id does not use the renamed column.
Every report that names the old column fails, not just one.

questions.prompt: Six changes are proposed: remove a column, rename a column, add an optional column, change a type from integer to text, change a price from tax included to tax excluded, and add a new table. How many of them are breaking for existing consumers?
hints: A change breaks a consumer if the old query stops working or returns something else.
A change of meaning counts.
Two of the six add something without changing what exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing, renaming, retyping and changing the meaning of a field are breaking, so 4. Adding an optional column and adding a table are compatible.

questions.onCorrect: A consumer relies on names, types and meaning, and any change to one of them can break it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the two compatible changes.
The change in meaning, tax included to tax excluded, breaks consumers too, even though the column keeps its name and type.

questions.prompt: A freshness objective is 99.9% of the time over a 30-day month, which is 720 hours. How many minutes of breach does the error budget allow?
hints: The allowed failure is 100% minus the objective.
0.1% of 720 hours.
Convert hours to minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The allowed failure is 0.1% of 720 hours, which is 0.72 hours, or 0.72 × 60 = 43.2 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: The budget shrinks fast as the objective tightens: each extra 9 divides it by ten.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the budget in hours. The question asks for minutes.
That is 1% of 720 hours. The failure allowed is 0.1%.

questions.prompt: Why is the error budget the period multiplied by one minus the objective?
hints: What share of the time may the data be late?

acceptedIdeas: The objective is the share that must work, so the rest may fail
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The objective is the share that must work, so the rest may fail

questions.onCorrect: The objective sets what must work, so the remainder, one minus the objective, is what may fail.

misconceptions.feedback: The 1% belongs to a 99% objective only. It changes with the objective.
A 99.5% objective does not mean that 99.5% of the time may fail.
The objective does not shorten the period.

choices.label: The objective is the share that must work, so the rest may fail
The budget is always 1% of the period
The objective is the time that may fail
The period is shortened by the objective

questions.prompt: The objective is 98% of the time over a 30-day month of 720 hours. How many hours of breach does the error budget allow?
hints: The allowed failure is 2% of the period.
Multiply the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2% of 720 hours is 0.02 × 720 = 14.4 hours.

questions.onCorrect: Loosening the objective by one point of percentage grows the budget by 7.2 hours in a 30-day month.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 0.2% of the period.
That is the time the objective requires to work, 98%.

questions.prompt: The sales team owns the meaning of order_total, and the platform team runs the scheduler. The meaning of order_total changes from gross to net. Who is accountable for telling consumers?
hints: Who decided that the meaning changes?

acceptedIdeas: The sales team, as the producer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sales team, as the producer

questions.onCorrect: The producing team owns the meaning, so it also owns telling the people who rely on it.

misconceptions.feedback: The platform team runs the tooling and does not decide what the field means.
Consumers rely on the producer to say so, and should not have to discover it.
That leaves nobody accountable, which is how a break goes unnoticed.

choices.label: The sales team, as the producer
The platform team, as it runs the pipeline
Each consumer, as it finds out
Whoever opens the dashboard next

questions.prompt: The objective is data ready by 07:00 on 90% of days over a 30-day month. Two days have already failed. How many more failed days can the month absorb before the objective is missed?
hints: The allowed failure is 10% of 30 days.
The budget is 3 days.
Subtract the days already failed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The budget is 10% of 30 days, which is 3 days. Two are spent, so 1 more can fail.

questions.onCorrect: The budget turns into a count of days that can still be spent before the objective is missed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole budget. Two days are already spent.
That is the number of days already failed.

questions.prompt: A producer makes five changes: renames a column, adds an optional column, changes a column's type from integer to string, adds a new table, and changes 'amount' from gross to net. How many are breaking?
hints: Rename, retype and change of meaning all alter what a consumer expects.
Adding something optional leaves the old fields as they were.
Count the changes that alter an existing field.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rename, the retyping and the change of meaning are breaking: 3. The optional column and the new table are compatible.

questions.onCorrect: Only changes to what already exists can break a consumer that expects the current schema.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the compatible ones.
Adding an optional column and adding a new table do not break existing consumers.

questions.prompt: A freshness objective is 99% of the time over a 30-day month (720 hours). How many hours of breach does the error budget allow?
hints: The allowed failure is 100% minus 99%.
1% of 720 hours.
Multiply 720 by 0.01.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1% of 720 hours is 0.01 × 720 = 7.2 hours.

questions.onCorrect: The budget is the failure the objective allows, and once it is spent the objective is missed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole month.
That is 0.1% of the month. The allowed failure is 1%.

questions.prompt: Which party owns the meaning of a dataset and should tell consumers when it changes: the producer, the consumer or the platform team? Answer with one word.
hints: It is the party that creates and publishes the dataset.
The platform team owns the tooling, not the meaning.
questions.onCorrect: The producing domain owns the meaning, and the platform team owns the tooling that checks it.

misconceptions.feedback: The platform team owns the tools and the scheduler. It does not decide what a field means.
A consumer relies on the meaning but does not set it.

questions.prompt: An email column is replaced by an unsalted hash of each email. Someone holds a list of 50,000 candidate emails and wants to find out which one belongs to a given hash. How many hashes must they compute, at most?
hints: Hash each candidate and compare.
One hash per candidate.
Count the candidates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They hash each candidate and compare, so at most 50,000 hashes are needed.

questions.onCorrect: The hash hides nothing from anyone who can guess the input, which makes it pseudonymisation at best.

misconceptions.feedback: One hash is not enough, since they do not know which candidate matches.
That squares the list. Each candidate needs one hash.

questions.prompt: A customer table has a column health_note holding free-text health information. Which of the labels public, internal, confidential and restricted fits it best? Answer with the label.
hints: Health information is among the most sensitive kinds.
It needs the strictest access and storage.
questions.onCorrect: GDPR treats health data as special category data, which earns the strictest label.

misconceptions.feedback: Confidential suits personal data such as an email. Health information needs more than that.

questions.prompt: Each of 1,000 records is hashed with its own random salt. An attacker wants to test 50,000 candidate emails against every record. How many hashes is that in the worst case?
hints: The salt differs for each record.
So the list must be hashed again for each record.
Multiply 50,000 by 1,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each record needs its own 50,000 hashes: 50,000 × 1,000 = 50,000,000.

questions.onCorrect: A per-record salt multiplies the attacker's work, but the data is still personal, because whoever holds the salts can link it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the work for unsalted data, where one pass of the list serves every record.
That counts the records only.

questions.prompt: In the nine-row table the groups have 4, 3, 1 and 1 rows. How many rows lie in groups smaller than 3?
hints: Find the groups with fewer than three rows.
Two groups have a single row.
Add their rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two groups of one row hold 1 + 1 = 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: Those rows are unique on the quasi-identifiers, so anyone who knows a person's age band, postcode and sex finds them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every row.
There are two single-row groups.

questions.prompt: Why is k the size of the smallest group and not the average group size?
hints: Which people are easiest to pick out?

acceptedIdeas: The smallest group holds the most exposed people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The smallest group holds the most exposed people

questions.onCorrect: A table is only as protected as its weakest group, so k takes the minimum.

misconceptions.feedback: The average can be computed, but a high average can hide a group of one.
The smallest group is not larger than the others.
How common a group is does not matter. Its size does.

choices.label: The smallest group holds the most exposed people
The average cannot be computed for groups
Small groups are always larger
The smallest group is the most common

questions.prompt: After widening the age band to 20-39, the six rows fall into groups (20-39, N1) with 3 rows and (20-39, N2) with 3 rows. What is k?
hints: k is the smallest group size.
Both groups have the same size.
Read the size off either group.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The smallest group has 3 rows, so k = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Widening a band merges groups, and here it lifts k from 1 to 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows in all.
Every group now has at least three rows.

questions.prompt: The nine-row table has groups of 4, 3, 1 and 1 rows. To reach k = 3 the rows in groups smaller than 3 are removed. How many rows remain?
hints: Remove the two single-row groups.
Subtract 2 from 9.
Check that 4 + 3 is the same.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 rows remain, in groups of 4 and 3.

questions.onCorrect: Suppression gives k = 3 at the cost of losing people from the data, which generalising avoids.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number removed.
Two rows are removed.

questions.prompt: Rows (age band, postcode prefix, sex): (30-39, LS1, F) x3; (40-49, LS2, M) x3; (20-29, LS1, M) x1; (30-39, LS1, M) x1. What is the k of this table?
hints: Count the rows in each group.
k is the smallest group size.
Two groups have a single row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The groups have 3, 3, 1 and 1 rows, and k is the smallest, 1.

questions.onCorrect: Two people are unique on these three columns, so the table is only 1-anonymous.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the largest groups. k is the smallest.
That is the number of rows that sit in small groups.

questions.prompt: For the same table, how many rows lie in groups smaller than 3 and so block k = 3?
hints: Find the groups with fewer than 3 rows.
Two groups have one row each.
Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two groups of one row hold 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: These two rows have to be generalised or removed for k to reach 3.

misconceptions.feedback: There are two single-row groups.
That is every row.

questions.prompt: Replacing an email with an unsalted hash of the email is an example of which technique, which still leaves personal data? Give the one word.
hints: The data can still be linked back, with extra information or by guessing.
Anonymisation would remove that possibility.
questions.onCorrect: Pseudonymised data stays personal data under GDPR, since it can be attributed to a person with additional information.

misconceptions.feedback: Anonymisation cannot be linked back to a person. A hash of a guessable email can.
Encryption can be reversed with a key. A hash cannot, but it can be guessed.

questions.prompt: A customer's rows are removed from a versioned lakehouse table with a DELETE. Three places held the data before: the current table, the old data files on storage, and the backups. How many of the three still hold it right after the DELETE?
hints: Which place does the DELETE change?
The table writes a new version and leaves the old files.
Backups are separate copies.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The current table no longer returns the rows, but the old files and the backups still hold them: 2 places.

questions.onCorrect: A DELETE in a versioned table is a new commit, and the data lives on in older files until they are vacuumed.

misconceptions.feedback: The DELETE changes the table's current version only. The old files stay on storage.
Both the old files and the backups still hold the data.

questions.prompt: Which principle says personal data must be kept no longer than needed for its purpose? Answer with its two-word name.
hints: It concerns how long data is kept.
The name is about limiting storage in time.
questions.onCorrect: It turns into a retention period and a job that deletes data when the period ends.

misconceptions.feedback: Data minimisation is about collecting only what is needed, not about how long it is kept.

questions.prompt: A company keeps invoices for seven years because tax law requires it. Which lawful basis fits? Answer with its name.
hints: The law, and not the customer, requires the processing.
One of the six bases is named for exactly this.
questions.onCorrect: Where the law requires the processing, consent is neither needed nor meaningful, because the person cannot refuse it.

misconceptions.feedback: Consent can be withdrawn, which would clash with a duty to keep the record.

questions.prompt: Which right lets a person receive their data in a common, machine-readable format to take elsewhere? Answer with its name.
hints: The person carries the data to another service.
The name is about moving data.
questions.onCorrect: In practice it is an export job that produces a standard format such as CSV or JSON.

misconceptions.feedback: Access gives the person a copy and information about the processing. The right asked about concerns a format that can be reused elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A DELETE is committed on day 2. The table keeps old files for a retention of 14 days. On what day is the earliest a vacuum can remove the old files?
hints: Retention counts from the commit.
Add the retention to the day of the commit.
2 plus 14.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The old files are kept for 14 days after the commit: day 2 + 14 = day 16.

questions.onCorrect: Until that day a time-travel query can still read the deleted rows, so the plan has to include the wait.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the retention alone. It starts counting from the commit on day 2.
That is when the DELETE happened, not when the files can go.

questions.prompt: Why does the data survive a DELETE in a versioned table?
hints: What does the table keep so that older versions can be read?

acceptedIdeas: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files in place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files in place

questions.onCorrect: Immutable files make time travel and recovery possible, which is why deleting for good takes more than a DELETE.

misconceptions.feedback: The timing of the DELETE is not the cause.
Nothing archives the rows. They stay where they were written.
The vacuum is what removes the old files, later.

choices.label: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files in place
The DELETE only runs at night
Deleted rows are archived automatically
The DELETE is cancelled by the vacuum

questions.prompt: A controller becomes aware of a breach at 14:00 on Monday, and wants to notify the authority within the 72-hour limit. It is now 14:00 on Tuesday. How many hours are left?
hints: The clock starts when the controller becomes aware.
One day has passed.
Take 24 from 72.
questions.onCorrect: The 72 hours run from awareness, not from the moment the breach happened.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time already used.
The clock started on Monday, so a day has already passed.

questions.prompt: The higher maximum fine for the most serious infringements is 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. A company has a turnover of 2.5 billion euros. What is the maximum, in millions of euros?
hints: Work out 4% of the turnover.
Compare it with 20 million.
The higher figure applies.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4% of 2,500 million is 100 million, which is more than 20 million, so the maximum is 100 million euros.

questions.onCorrect: The turnover limb lets the ceiling scale with the size of a company.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fixed amount, and the higher of the two applies.
That is 4% of 250 million, one tenth of the turnover.

questions.prompt: How many lawful bases for processing does the GDPR list?
hints: Consent is one of them.
Contract and legal obligation are others.
There are consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Article 6 lists six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.

questions.onCorrect: Consent is only one of six, which is why it is often the wrong basis to reach for.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the seven principles. The lawful bases are six.
There are six bases.

questions.prompt: Within how many hours of becoming aware should a controller, where feasible, notify the authority of a personal data breach?
hints: It is a number of hours stated in Article 33.
It equals three days.
Seventy-two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Article 33 sets 72 hours from becoming aware, where feasible.

questions.onCorrect: If the notice is later than that, it has to say why.

misconceptions.feedback: The limit is three days.
That is the time left a day after awareness, not the limit.

questions.prompt: A customer's rows are deleted from a versioned lakehouse table with a DELETE. Which operation, run after the retention period, actually removes the old data files? Give the one word.
hints: The DELETE leaves old files, which another command cleans up.
The command is named for cleaning up.
questions.onCorrect: Backups still have to expire as well, so a full erasure plan covers the table, its old files and its backups.

misconceptions.feedback: The DELETE has already run. It writes a new version and leaves the old files.

questions.prompt: A retention policy says that data older than 36 months must be deleted. A table holds one monthly partition for each of the last 40 months. How many partitions should a correct retention job delete?
hints: The policy keeps 36 months.
Subtract what is kept from what is there.
40 minus 36.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Months 37 to 40 are older than 36 months, so 40 − 36 = 4 partitions.

questions.onCorrect: The rule is exact, so a job and a check can enforce it without anyone having to remember.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of partitions the policy keeps.
That is the whole table.

questions.prompt: In a team, one analyst writes and maintains the definition of 'headcount' and watches its day-to-day quality, while the HR director is accountable for the dataset. What is the analyst's role called?
hints: The analyst is not accountable for the dataset, and does not run the platform.
The role looks after definitions and quality in practice.
questions.onCorrect: The steward keeps the definitions and day-to-day quality, while the owner is accountable for the dataset.

misconceptions.feedback: The owner is accountable for the dataset. The analyst maintains its definitions.
The custodian runs the platform that stores the data.

questions.prompt: A catalogue records what a dataset means and who is accountable for it, in words written by a person. Is a description of this kind technical, business or operational metadata? Answer with one word.
hints: Technical metadata describes structure, and operational metadata describes behaviour.
This kind says what the data means.
questions.onCorrect: Business metadata carries meaning, such as the owner, the description and the glossary term, and needs a person to write it.

misconceptions.feedback: Technical metadata describes structure, such as the schema and the data types.
Operational metadata describes behaviour, such as refresh time, row count and usage.

questions.prompt: A table holds one row for each of the last 48 months, and a 36-month retention job runs. How many rows does the job delete?
hints: The job keeps 36 months.
Subtract the kept months from 48.
48 minus 36.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 48 − 36 = 12 rows are older than 36 months.

questions.onCorrect: The check that follows counts rows older than 36 months, and should return none.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number kept.
That is the whole table.

questions.prompt: Why is a written policy that salary is visible only to HR not enough on its own?
hints: What happens if someone has not read the policy?

acceptedIdeas: Nothing stops a person who ignores it, whereas a masking rule does
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing stops a person who ignores it, whereas a masking rule does

questions.onCorrect: A control enforces the rule whoever is at the keyboard, and a monitor shows if it ever fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Policies can be written. Without a control they depend on people remembering them.
Salary is personal data, which is why access to it is limited.
A policy can be current. The weakness is that nothing enforces it.

choices.label: Nothing stops a person who ignores it, whereas a masking rule does
Policies are not legally allowed
Salary is not personal data
Written policies are always out of date

questions.prompt: A table holds one row for each of the last 26 months, and an 18-month retention job runs. How many rows does the job delete?
hints: The job keeps 18 months.
Subtract.
26 minus 18.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 26 − 18 = 8 rows are older than 18 months.

questions.onCorrect: A retention rule is a number, so the job, the check and the evidence all follow from it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number kept.
That is the whole table.

questions.prompt: Certification needs six conditions: an owner, a glossary definition, passing tests, freshness within its objective, a classification, and visible lineage. A dataset has an owner, a definition, passing tests and visible lineage. How many conditions does it still lack?
hints: Count the conditions met.
Subtract them from the total.
6 minus 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 − 4 = 2: freshness within its objective, and a classification.

questions.onCorrect: Each condition is something an earlier lesson showed how to produce, from tests to lineage to classification.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number met.
That is the number needed.

questions.prompt: A catalogue lists 40 datasets, and 25 of them have a named owner. How many datasets still need an owner?
hints: Count what is missing.
Subtract those with an owner from the total.
40 minus 25.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 − 25 = 15 datasets.

questions.onCorrect: A dataset without an owner has nobody accountable, so owner coverage is a number a governance process can track.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number that already have one.
That is the percentage with an owner, not the count that lack one.

questions.prompt: Which role is accountable for a dataset's use and quality targets: the data owner, the data custodian or the data consumer? Answer with the role.
hints: It is the role that answers for the dataset.
The custodian runs the platform and the consumer uses the data.
questions.onCorrect: The owner is accountable, the steward maintains definitions and quality, and the custodian runs the platform.

misconceptions.feedback: The custodian runs the platform that stores the data. It is not accountable for how the data is used.
A consumer uses the data and depends on targets that someone else sets.

questions.prompt: Last refresh time and row count are which kind of metadata: technical, business or operational? Answer with one word.
hints: They describe how the dataset behaves, not what it is.
They change each time the data is refreshed.
questions.onCorrect: Operational metadata describes behaviour, and a catalogue can collect it automatically.

misconceptions.feedback: Technical metadata describes structure, such as the schema.
Business metadata describes meaning, such as the owner and glossary term.

questions.prompt: A 24-month retention policy is turned into a scheduled delete of rows older than 24 months. A table holds one row for each of the last 30 months. How many rows does the delete remove?
hints: The job keeps 24 months.
Subtract the kept months from 30.
30 minus 24.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 − 24 = 6 rows are older than 24 months.

questions.onCorrect: The policy has become a job, and a check that counts rows older than 24 months should then find none.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number kept.
That is the whole table.

flashcards.front: A line table repeats each order total on every line. Orders of 50 and 70 have 2 and 3 lines. What does SUM(order_total) return?
flashcards.back: 50 × 2 + 70 × 3 = 310, against 120 for the two orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 × 2 + 70 × 3 = 310, against 120 for the two orders.

flashcards.front: Name the first of the four design steps. It is the thing you choose before the grain.
flashcards.back: Everything else follows from the activity the question is about, so it is chosen first.

flashcards.front: Why must every column of a fact table be true at its declared grain?
flashcards.back: Because a row stands for one definite thing, and a column that describes something larger gets repeated on several rows and inflates any sum.

flashcards.front: Daily stock of product P3 was 12, 18 and 10. What is the end-of-period value?
flashcards.back: The end-of-period value is the last day's figure, 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The end-of-period value is the last day's figure, 10.

flashcards.front: Which kind of fact table has one row per product per day, whether or not anything happened?
flashcards.back: It records state at regular intervals, such as stock levels or balances.

flashcards.front: Why does a dimension carry a surrogate key as well as the source system's id?
flashcards.back: Source ids can repeat across systems, change, or lose history, whereas a key owned by the warehouse stays stable.

flashcards.front: A Type 2 dimension marks its current row with a far-future valid_to. Which date does this course use? Write it as yyyy-mm-dd.
flashcards.back: A far-future date marks the open-ended current version, and a query can find current rows by it.

flashcards.front: An attribute of one customer changes 3 times under Type 2. How many rows does the customer have, counting the original?
flashcards.back: The original row plus one new row per change gives 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The original row plus one new row per change gives 4.

flashcards.front: Why join a fact to the dimension row valid on the fact's date rather than to the current row?
flashcards.back: Because the current row describes the present, and past facts need the attribute value that was true when they happened.

flashcards.front: Customers with credit limits 500 and 100 have 2 and 3 orders. Joined to orders, what does SUM(credit_limit) return?
In a data vault, which kind of table holds the history of descriptive attributes?
flashcards.back: Hubs hold keys and links hold relationships, so descriptive history lives in satellites.

flashcards.front: Why is a star usually the best shape for reporting, and a vault for integration?
flashcards.back: A star makes reading simple and fast with one join per attribute, whereas a vault keeps keys, relationships and history apart so many sources can be integrated and audited.

flashcards.front: Which materialisation stores no data and runs its query each time the model is read?
flashcards.back: A view costs nothing to build but pays when it is read.

flashcards.front: A mart depends on two intermediate models, each of which depends on two different staging models, all distinct. How many models must run before the mart?
flashcards.back: 2 intermediate + 4 staging = 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 intermediate + 4 staging = 6.

flashcards.front: Why do staging models do nothing except rename and retype?
flashcards.back: So that every later model sees the same cleaned source, and a change in the source is fixed in one place.

flashcards.front: Which operation rebuilds an incremental model from scratch, repairing old rows after a change of logic? Two words.
flashcards.back: It reprocesses every row, so it fixes rows the filter would never read again.

flashcards.front: The target's latest updated_at is 2026-06-20 and the lookback is 3 days. Rows later than which day of June are read? Give the day number.
flashcards.back: 20 minus 3 is 17, so rows after 2026-06-17 are read.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 minus 3 is 17, so rows after 2026-06-17 are read.

flashcards.front: Why does a unique key alone not catch a late-arriving row?
flashcards.back: The key only stops duplicates among rows that are read, and the filter has to read the late row first.

flashcards.front: A data test returns no rows. Does it pass or fail?
flashcards.back: A test is written to return the rows that break the rule, so no rows means nothing broke.

flashcards.front: Which standard test checks that every value of a column is on a given list?
flashcards.back: Its failing rows are those whose value is not on the list.

flashcards.front: Why test the sources and staging models as well as the final marts?
flashcards.back: A failure is cheapest to explain closest to its cause, and by the mart it may be several models and hours away.

flashcards.front: Revenue is 600 from 20 orders in one region and 400 from 30 orders in another. What is the overall average order value?
Which kind of metric divides one metric by another, such as average order value?
flashcards.back: It stores a numerator and a denominator and divides after aggregating them.

flashcards.front: Why can distinct customers not be added across regions?
flashcards.back: A customer who appears in two regions is counted once in each, so the sum counts that customer twice, and the distinct count has to be recomputed.

flashcards.front: A source feeds a staging model, which feeds two marts, each of which feeds one different dashboard. How many nodes are downstream of the staging model?
flashcards.back: 2 marts and 2 dashboards: 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 marts and 2 dashboards: 4.

flashcards.front: Name the activity of walking downstream from a changing node to list what it can break.
flashcards.back: It lists the models, reports and owners that a change reaches.

flashcards.front: Why is lineage captured from runs rather than drawn by hand?
flashcards.back: A drawing goes out of date when jobs change, whereas events emitted by each run describe what actually read and wrote what.

flashcards.front: The mean count is 50, the population standard deviation is 5, and today's count is 65. What is the z-score?
Which quality dimension asks whether every required value is present?
flashcards.back: It is measured as non-null rows over all rows.

flashcards.front: Why is data quality reported as a rate against a target and not as pass or fail?
flashcards.back: No dataset is perfect, and what counts as good enough depends on the use, so a rate shows how far a dataset is from the target for that use.

flashcards.front: A freshness objective is 99.5% over a 30-day month (720 hours). How many hours of breach does the budget allow?
flashcards.back: 0.5% of 720 hours is 3.6 hours.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.5% of 720 hours is 3.6 hours.

flashcards.front: Which kind of change, such as renaming a column, makes an existing consumer fail?
flashcards.back: A consumer relies on the existing names, types and meaning.

flashcards.front: Why does a data contract have to be checked by a machine?
flashcards.back: An agreement kept only in a document drifts from the data, whereas a check on every build or run shows at once when it is broken.

flashcards.front: Which label fits a column of public product names?
flashcards.back: Anyone may see it, so it needs no restriction.

flashcards.front: A table has groups of 5, 2 and 4 rows on its quasi-identifiers. What is k?
flashcards.back: k is the smallest group size, 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: k is the smallest group size, 2.

flashcards.front: Why is a table with the names removed not necessarily anonymous?
flashcards.back: Ordinary columns such as age band, postcode and sex can together single a person out, so a person may still be identified.

flashcards.front: How many principles does Article 5 of the GDPR set out, counting accountability?
flashcards.back: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability make 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability make 7.

flashcards.front: Name the lawful basis used when processing is needed to perform a contract with the person.
flashcards.back: Shipping an ordered parcel is an example.

flashcards.front: Why is a SQL DELETE not the end of an erasure in a versioned table?
flashcards.back: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files and backups, which hold the data until they are vacuumed and expire.

flashcards.front: Which governance role runs the platform that stores a dataset?
flashcards.back: The custodian looks after storage and protection, while the owner is accountable and the steward maintains definitions.

flashcards.front: A catalogue lists 20 datasets and 15 have a named owner. How many still need one?
Take the policy "customer emails are visible only to support staff". Name the control that would enforce it.
flashcards.back: A good answer names a control that the platform enforces, such as masking the email column for every role except support, and a check or log that shows it working.
